I.

INTRODUCTION:

[
1
]

Michael
Geluch claims damages of approximately $475,000 from his former employer, the
Rosedale Golf Club Association (“Rosedale”), alleging breach of his contract of
employment and wrongful dismissal.  Rosedale disputes the claim and asserts
that Mr. Geluch was dismissed for cause, that no notice was required and that
no compensation is owed.  It also advances a counterclaim for monies it says
are owed by Mr. Geluch.

II.

FACTUAL BACKGROUND:

[
2
]

Michael
Geluch was hired by Rosedale in 1985 to serve as General Manager and
Secretary/Treasurer.  Rosedale, which has been in existence
for over one hundred years, is operated by a voluntary board, whose members
rotate every year.  When Mr. Geluch was hired, he was the fourth General
Manager in Rosedale’s history.  Mr. Geluch’s predecessor had occupied his
position for thirty-seven years.

[
3
]

The
plaintiff had been General Manager at the York Downs Golf and Country Club for
eleven years when he was approached to apply for the position at Rosedale.  He
had studied hotel and restaurant management at Ryerson University, and had
previous experience as a Clubhouse Manager, and later as a General Manager at
two other golf clubs.  His employment at York Downs seemed to be secure and Mr.
Geluch had a good relationship with its Board, membership and staff.

[
4
]

During
the interview for the position at Rosedale, Mr. Geluch says that he was told by
the headhunter, Price Waterhouse, that he would be the fourth General Manager
of the Club.  He says that this was repeated when he met with the members of
the Board of Directors.  Mr. Geluch claims that he relied on their
representations that he would be embarking upon long-term employment when he
accepted the position.  In fact, in the engagement letter offering Mr. Geluch a
position at Rosedale, the President wrote that the Club looked forward to “many
years of contribution and service.”  Mr. Geluch claims that his job security
was extremely important to him as he was married and, at the time, had two
young children.

[
5
]

When the
plaintiff started his employment at Rosedale on December 1, 1985, he was
earning an annual salary of $65,000, paid on a bi-weekly basis, plus benefits.
In addition to his regular salary, Mr. Geluch was paid an educational allowance
that covered the cost of attending national and international conferences of the
Canadian and American Associations of Club Managers.  He attended monthly
meetings and educational courses offered by those organizations.  Mr. Geluch
was also paid a car allowance.  He was entitled to spend up to $3,000 per year

to entertain guests.  At the outset, that amount was to be used at
Rosedale, but, in the late 1980’s, it was extended to allow him to entertain
and expense for business items purchased outside Rosedale.  Mr. Geluch
testified that it was understood that, since he was responsible for the quality
of food and wine at Rosedale, it would benefit Rosedale for him to go outside
the facility.

[
6
]

The
plaintiff’s responsibilities as General Manager included: overseeing the golf
course and operations, overseeing the food and beverage and catering services,
supervising staff, preparing budgets, and working closely with the Board of
Directors to carry out the operations of the Club.  Rosedale’s Board consisted
of twelve members, four of whom were elected each year, with the President
elected annually.  As Secretary/Treasurer, Mr. Geluch was required to take
minutes at meetings and to present financial information to the Finance
Committee.  He was an
ex officio
member of all committees and took
minutes for all committees.  The General Manager provided continuity for the
Board, given the constant change in membership.

[
7
]

Mr. Geluch
was also very visible to members at the club.  He worked five-and-a-half to six
days a week, came in on Saturday mornings, had meals in the dining room, and
attended all events.

[
8
]

The
plaintiff saw that one of his challenges was to improve the quality of food and
wine offered in the restaurants and catering services, and he took a sincere
interest in this aspect of the operation.  He testified that he tried to make
Rosedale unique.  An example of one of his initiatives was to serve and sell
ginger snap cookies to Club members; another was to provide catering of special
meals such as turkey dinners at Christmas.  Mr. Geluch took an active role in
special activities, such as the celebration of Rosedale’s centennial year, and
was instrumental in the publication of a book marking that occasion.

[
9
]

Each year,
Mr. Geluch met with the Executive Committee to review the performance of the
Senior Management group and to decide on salary increases for the next year.
His performance was reviewed by the President and Vice President, and they
determined any salary changes.  Mr. Geluch reported to the Office Manager,
Violet Nettleton, what the individual increases would be for all staff,
including his own.  The criteria upon which Mr. Geluch was assessed were:
maintaining the image and integrity of Rosedale, managing the 120 staff
members, managing financial operations (overseeing payroll, expense accounts
and financial statements), and maintaining relations with members and with the
Board.

[
10
]

In October 1997, it was brought to
the attention of Board members Frank Newbould (who was Chair of the House
Committee that was responsible for personnel issues in the operation of the
Club House) and Paul Cowie (who was President), that Anne Taylor, a former
employee of Rosedale for ten years, had a story to tell about the reason for
her departure from the Club.  Ms. Taylor had been hired by Mr. Geluch in June
1987 to manage the informal dining area.  She had left Rosedale to take
employment as Clubhouse Manager at another Toronto golf club, and most people
assumed she left in order to receive a promotion.

[
11
]

Mr. Newbould contacted Anne Taylor
and arranged to meet with her at the Albany Club in Toronto on October 28,
1997.  Mr. Newbould testified that Ms. Taylor was initially very reluctant to
speak with him, but after she was reassured that the nature of the conversation
would not be disclosed without her permission, and that Rosedale would
compensate her if there were any repercussions for her with respect to her
employment, she agreed to meet with them and told them about certain incidents
involving Mr. Geluch.

[
12
]

Ms. Taylor described Mr. Geluch’s
conduct towards her as abusive, belittling and degrading, especially in the
latter years of her employment.  She provided certain examples.  After Ms.
Taylor recounted these events, Mr. Newbould went back to his office, which was
close by, to dictate the notes of their conversation.  Mr. Cowie convened a
meeting of the Board members on short notice, held on October 30, 1997 at his
house.  Mr. Newbould and Mr. Cowie reported to the other Board members what
they had learned from Ms. Taylor concerning Mr. Geluch.  The Board voted to
dismiss Mr. Geluch immediately and made interim arrangements for the management
of Rosedale.  Mr. Cowie contacted Mr. Geluch on October 30, 1997 and arranged
to meet with him at 4:00 p.m. the following day, at his office.  Mr. Geluch was
not told the purpose of the meeting set for October 31.

[
13
]

A staff party for the retirement
of a longstanding employee was underway on the afternoon of Friday, October 31,
1997.  Mr. Geluch left the party to meet with Mr. Cowie at 4:00 p.m., and was
surprised to see that Mr. John

Hearne (another Board member) and Mr.
Newbould were also present.  Mr. Cowie informed Mr. Geluch that Rosedale had
lost confidence in his ability as General Manager and that he was being
dismissed immediately.  He was given a letter confirming the termination of his
employment.  Mr. Geluch was asked to forfeit his keys and cards.  Mr. Geluch
says that, instead of speaking to him or investigating the matter or suspending
him with pay, the Board members convened a special meeting and terminated his
employment on the spot.

[
14
]

Several employees witnessed Mr.
Geluch’s dismissal and subsequent departure from Rosedale.  Kathleen Mannion,
who was the Clubhouse Manager at the time, testified that she saw Mr. Cowie
waiting in the General Manager’s office for the locksmith.  She observed that
other employees could also see him there, and wondered what was going on.
Michael Rosano, the Executive Chef at Rosedale at the time, testified that, at
the time that Mr. Geluch was dismissed, staff members were going in and out of
the room across from Mr. Geluch’s office to attend the retirement party.  While
he was there, Mr. Romano observed something going on in Mr. Geluch’s office and
saw him being escorted out of the building by the Board members.

[
15
]

By the time he left his employment
at Rosedale in 1997, Mr. Geluch was responsible for an annual budget of
approximately $6 million.  He had overseen major capital improvements to the
clubhouse and to the golf course.  The quality of food and catering had
improved substantially.  At the time of his dismissal, Mr. Geluch was earning
an annual salary of approximately $129,000, which Mr. Geluch says included an
annual

clothing allowance of $2,000 and an annual car allowance of
$8,000.  He received health and medical benefits and was entitled to five
weeks’ vacation, and the employer’s contribution to his pension was six to
seven per cent of his base salary.

[
16
]

Mr. Geluch attempted to find other
employment when he left Rosedale.  It took thirteen months before he was
offered a job as General Manager by the Seymour Golf and Country Club in
Vancouver.  In January 2004, he left that employment.  He now resides in North
Vancouver, British Columbia.

III.

ISSUES:

[
17
]

The following issues arise in this
case:

1. Was Mr. Geluch wrongfully dismissed by Rosedale?

2. If so, what is the appropriate period of notice?

3. Is Mr. Geluch entitled to damages?

4. Is Rosedale entitled to damages by way of counterclaim?

IV.

POSITIONS OF THE PARTIES:

[
18
]

Both parties agree that Mr. Geluch
owed his employer a duty of fidelity, that he occupied a fiduciary role, that
he was bound by Rosedale’s policy regarding dismissal for cause, that Rosedale
had a sexual harassment policy in place when Mr. Geluch was employed there and
that Mr. Geluch had the responsibility of notifying employees about the
existence of that policy.

[
19
]

Mr. Geluch says that he had a
contract of employment with Rosedale that was open-ended, that he relied upon
Rosedale’s representations that the employment would be for a lengthy period of
time, and that he was dismissed without just cause.  Mr. Geluch claims that during
the twelve years he spent at Rosedale, he had an excellent relationship with
the Club’s members, with Board members and with the approximately 120 staff for
whom Mr. Geluch was responsible.  He argues that he was entitled to reasonable
notice, and that the notice period should have been eighteen months.  He seeks
damages reflecting what would have been his salary and benefits during that
period, additional damages for the manner of his dismissal and for high-handed
conduct on the part of the Board members, and punitive damages.

[
20
]

Rosedale takes the position that
Mr. Geluch was dismissed for just cause.    Reasons were not provided to Mr.
Geluch at the time of the dismissal, but the allegations later disclosed may be
summarized as follows:

1.

Abuse
of staff;

2.

Improper
credit card expenses;

3.

Unauthorized
salary increases;

4.

Unauthorized
taking of food and wine;

5.

Sexual
harassment; and

6.

Withholding
of financial information from the Board of Directors.

Rosedale
submits that these allegations, both individually and collectively, amount to
just cause for dismissal.

[
21
]

Rosedale also submits that this is
a case about credibility and that, during the trial, Mr. Geluch’s credibility
was impeached.  Counsel points out numerous inconsistencies in his evidence to
suggest that his evidence should not be believed.

V.

WAS MR. GELUCH WRONGFULLY DISMISSED BY ROSEDALE?

a.

The
Allegations of Cause:

[
22
]

The letter terminating Mr.
Geluch’s employment indicated only that he was being dismissed and that
Rosedale had lost confidence in his management.  Although Mr. Geluch was told
that Rosedale wanted to work out his dismissal with him and settle the matter,
it was also suggested to him that he might want to resign rather than be
dismissed.  Mr. Geluch was given ten minutes to decide whether or not to resign,
at which point he told the Board members that he was not prepared to resign.
Mr. Geluch says that he was not permitted the opportunity to say goodbye to his
employees.  He handed over his master keys and credit card and was escorted off
the premises.  Mr. Geluch was paid his salary for two months on a “without
prejudice basis”.  He says that he was not advised that his remuneration would
cease two months after the dismissal, which it did.

[
23
]

Following his dismissal, Mr.
Geluch hired a lawyer to negotiate with Rosedale.  In a letter dated December
13, 1997, his lawyer was told by Rosedale’s lawyer that Mr. Geluch had been
fired for cause and that the reasons were as follows:

1.

He
shouted at, berated and swore at staff, whose health was affected;

2.

There
was evidence that he took food and liquor;

3.

He
had employees do work for him personally, for which he didn’t pay;

4.

He
used the Club credit card for personal expenses; and

5.

There
was improper recording of accounts receivable.

[
24
]

At that time, no mention was made
of any allegations of sexual harassment.  Mr. Geluch continued to seek
particulars regarding cause in January 1998.  There were various meetings and
discussions, but no resolution was achieved.  Mr. Geluch commenced this claim
on July 27, 1998.

[
25
]

At trial, in order to demonstrate
that it had just cause to dismiss Mr. Geluch, Rosedale presented evidence and
called witnesses to testify about various allegations of misconduct on the part
of Mr. Geluch.  These included allegations of (1) fiscal impropriety, (2) theft,
and (3) abusive conduct towards staff.  Mr. Geluch, for his part, presented
evidence and called witnesses to testify in order to refute those allegations,
as well as to support what Mr. Geluch submits was the “real” reason behind his
dismissal.  I now consider all of these allegations, in turn.

i.

Fiscal Impropriety:

[
26
]

Rosedale alleges that, during his
employment at Rosedale, Mr. Geluch committed numerous acts of fiscal
impropriety.  After Mr. Geluch was dismissed, Rosedale decided to investigate
financial matters at the Club and instructed their auditor, Marion MacDonald,
from the firm of Hillborn Ellis & Grant, which had replaced the accounting
firm of KPMG in 1996, to conduct an investigation and to prepare a report
reviewing credit card purchases made by Mr. Geluch for the years 1993 to 1997.
The assignment was not an audit, but entailed reviewing credit card statements,
cash disbursements and cash receipts, allocating items for which Mr. Geluch had
been reimbursed and categorizing the amounts as “business” or “personal”.  In
this limited capacity, the accounting firm was performing what was described as
a “related” service involving a compilation of financial information, but it
was not an “assurance” service.

[
27
]

Ms. MacDonald relied upon three
accounts from the general ledgers to arrive at her conclusions.  Copies of all
the general ledger accounts except those three for the years 1994 to 1997 were
missing without explanation.  Nonetheless, Ms. MacDonald drew conclusions based
upon what was available.

[
28
]

According to Mr. Geluch, there
were numerous errors in Ms. MacDonald’s categorization of expenses, and the
expenses that were noted as personal were all paid back by him.  However, this
is not reflected in the general ledger cash disbursements account.

[
29
]

Next, Rosedale relied on the
allegations of Violet Nettleton.  Ms. Nettleton worked as the Office Manager at
Rosedale for fourteen years, but took early retirement in February 2000, at the
age of fifty-nine, when it was recommended by the new General Manager that she
leave.  She was paid fifteen months’ severance.  Ms. Nettleton was told of Mr.
Geluch’s dismissal on the day he was fired.  She was contacted by Mr. Newbould
and agreed to meet with him on November 30, 1997.

[
30
]

Ms. Nettleton had been hired by
Mr. Geluch.  As Office Manager, her duties were to send out member statements,
to oversee payroll, accounts payable and accounts receivable, and to perform
secretarial functions.  She reported directly to Mr. Geluch.

[
31
]

Ms. Nettleton stated that, in
early 1997, following the salary increases approved by the Board of Directors
at their meeting on December 1, the bookkeeper had been instructed by Mr.
Geluch to write two cheques of $4,000 each, as an advance payment to Mr. Geluch
of an $8,000 salary increase for the year.  The cheques were written in amounts
less than $5,000 so as not to require a director’s signature.

[
32
]

Mr. Geluch’s explanation was that
it was difficult to find one of the three directors who had signing authority
to sign cheques over Christmas and early in the winter, and that he wanted to
receive the money quickly, as his son was getting married.  There is no
question that the payments were properly recorded, and Mr. Geluch testified
that he paid income tax on them.

[
33
]

In his evidence, Mr. Geluch said
that, had he known that it would be a problem, he would have waited and asked a
Director to sign the cheques.   He says that he never took a salary advance
before or after the incident early in 1997.  He says that he had no intention
to deceive the Board of Directors.  He acknowledged that he was always paid on
a bi-weekly basis and that had never changed.

[
34
]

Mr. Geluch acknowledged that
taking his increase in this fashion may have been an error in judgment.
Certainly, this was not the first time that the bookkeeper had written two
cheques in order to avoid the requirement of a Director’s signature during the
winter months.  However, he acknowledged that he did not have the Board of
Directors’ approval to take a salary advance.

ii.

Theft:

[
35
]

Rosedale interviewed several former
employees, and catalogued their grievances about Mr. Geluch.  Those grievances
were raised at trial, as justification for Mr. Geluch’s dismissal.

[
36
]

Several of the witnesses testified
that they had seen Mr. Geluch take supplies or material from Rosedale during of
his employment.  Ms. Nettleton said that she had seen Mr. Geluch take food and
wine for his own consumption without reimbursing the Club.  Melva Buell, a
former Executive Chef, also said that she saw Mr. Geluch take food and wine
from the Club, and that he would have her prepare foods for him to entertain
others at home.  She says that she kept a log of costs, but no record was
produced in court.  She could not say whether the food and wine was taken for
personal or business purposes.

[
37
]

Ross Irwin was the Supervisor of
Maintenance at Rosedale until his retirement in 1999.  He had been hired by Mr.
Geluch and had worked at the Club since 1986.  His responsibilities included
general maintenance and woodworking.  Mr. Irwin was approached following Mr.
Geluch’s dismissal, and interviewed by Mr. Newbould.

[
38
]

Mr. Irwin said that he had been
asked by Mr. Geluch to build certain items while working at Rosedale, for which
he used materials purchased by Rosedale.  The items included: a folding table
for Mr. Geluch’s kitchen at home, ski racks for his garage, kitchen cupboards
and an antique creamery table.  Mr. Irwin testified that he built ten flower
boxes with a special design done without nails or screws, only six of which
were used at Rosedale.  Mr. Irwin said that he later saw two such boxes at Mr.
Geluch’s house, and that he never saw the other two boxes.  In
cross-examination, however, he was not able to say where Mr. Geluch resided.
He denied that Mr. Geluch paid for anything that he built for him.  Mr. Irwin
also testified that he removed a radio from Mr. Geluch’s car during work hours
while the car was parked in the Rosedale parking lot.  The car was being sold
by Mr. Geluch.

[
39
]

At trial, Mr. Geluch conceded that
Mr. Irwin built items for the office and that he had built some items for Mr.
Geluch personally.  Those included a small kitchen table that folded into the
wall, and a ski rack.  Mr. Geluch says that he paid Mr. Irwin in cash for the
table, and that the ski rack was made from scrap lumber.  Mr. Geluch did not
concern himself about when Mr. Irwin was working on items for him.  As for
re-finishing the creamery table, Mr. Geluch says that he brought the table to
work, asked Mr. Irwin how to finish it and borrowed his tools in order to the
do the job himself.  Mr. Geluch denied that Mr. Irwin took the radio out of his
car and says that he sold the car with the radio in it.  As for the flower
boxes, Mr. Geluch says that each box cost approximately $30 to $40, and that he
did not take any of the boxes for his own use.

iii.

Abusive Conduct Towards Staff:

[
40
]

Rosedale also submitted that
former employees were afraid of Mr. Geluch, and that they were afraid to speak
to Board members about their concerns, for fear of losing their jobs.  However,
Rosedale interviewed several former employees who spoke out about inappropriate
or abusive treatment they suffered at the hands of Mr. Geluch.

[
41
]

Anne Taylor was a former Clubhouse
Manager at Rosedale.  She met with Frank Newbould and Paul Cowie, and recounted
several incidents involving Mr. Geluch.  These incidents were of great concern
to Mr. Newbould and to Mr. Cowie.  In fact, according to Mr. Newbould, who was
the Chair of Rosedale’s House Committee for the 1996-1997 term, and was
responsible for personnel matters, the allegations of Anne Taylor were the sole
reasons for the dismissal of Mr. Geluch.

[
42
]

In 1989, the informal dining room,
known as the Terrace Room, was re-opened following its renovation, and a number
of new kitchen staff were hired.  Management made an announcement to members
about the re-opening and, on the night of the re-opening, the dining room was
packed.  The kitchen was overwhelmed and it was taking a great deal of time for
food to be prepared.  According to Ms. Taylor, Mr. Geluch had brought some guests
to the opening event and he was frustrated with the delay in service.  She said
that he approached her, poked her on the shoulder and said, “This is your
fault. Fix it.”  At approximately 9:15 p.m. that evening, he called her into
his office.  She said that Mr. Geluch berated her and said, “That was the most
disgusting display that I’ve seen of a manager. You’re nothing more than a
glorified waitress.”

[
43
]

Ms. Taylor was so upset that night
that she was crying, and she stopped at Violet Nettleton’s house on her way
home from work.  She told Ms. Nettleton what had happened and remained there
for approximately an hour until she was able to drive home.  The conduct of
poking her on the shoulder was described in the notes of Mr. Newbould as
“physically abusive”.

[
44
]

In a second incident, during a
Christmas party at which her father was dressed as Santa Claus, Ms. Taylor says
that Mr. Geluch berated her in front of her father, for taking photographs
instead of concerning herself with the food.  She was upset by the incident,
and upset that Mr. Geluch did not thank her father for serving as Santa Claus,
nor did he provide him with drink or food.

[
45
]

A third incident occurred in 1993
when Rosedale was celebrating its centennial and Ms. Taylor was dressed in
costume.  The Terrace Room was decorated as a “Wild West” saloon and she was
dressed as Rosie and was wearing a low cut dress with a tattoo of a rose
painted on her chest.  She says that Mr. Geluch made a derogatory remark to her
along the lines of, “You call those breasts?”    Ms. Taylor said that she did
not know whether Mr. Geluch was joking or whether he was angry.  Mr. Geluch
denied saying this to her.

[
46
]

Ms. Taylor left Rosedale to take a
job as Clubhouse Manager at another club, which was a promotion.  There was a
going away party for her and she received a gift from the staff.  Although she
did not tell others this when she left, she later said that she left Rosedale
because she did not want to work with Michael Geluch or Kathleen Mannion any
longer.  However, she also admitted that she left Rosedale for a better
position as Clubhouse Manager at another golf club.

[
47
]

Ms. Taylor told Mr. Newbould and
Mr. Cowie that staff members were afraid to speak to anyone about Mr. Geluch’s
behaviour, as they feared they would be dismissed.  Ms. Taylor also said that
other employees, such as Violet Nettleton, the Office Manager, and Melva Buell,
the Executive Chef, were berated by Mr. Geluch in front of other staff and
brought to tears.  Ms. Taylor admitted that she only discussed these incidents
because Mr. Newbould had contacted her.  Ms. Taylor never made a complaint
about her treatment by Mr. Geluch to her supervisor, Kathleen Mannion, or to
any members, before she left Rosedale.  She agreed that she had a good
relationship with Ms. Mannion.

[
48
]

On November 30, 1997, Mr. Newbould
met with Melva Buell, a former Executive Chef, who had worked at Rosedale from
April 1992 until March 1996.  Ms. Buell had been hired by Mr. Geluch and had
been asked to update the menu and provide upscale food for the restaurants and
catering.

[
49
]

Ms. Buell
testified that she loved working at Rosedale and enjoyed the challenge.
However, she found the work to be stressful.  At the beginning, her
relationship with Mr. Geluch was fine but, as time went on, she found it
difficult to work there.  There were a few incidents that upset her and she
says that they caused her to resign.  Ms. Buell recounted those incidents to
Mr. Newbould.  They are summarized below.

[
50
]

In 1992,
following a dinner sponsored by the Canadian Food and Beverage Association that
both she and Mr. Geluch attended, Mr. Geluch drove Ms. Buell home.  She said
that, as she was getting out of the car, being a friendly person, she leaned
across to say good night, put her hand on Mr. Geluch’s arm and thanked him for
the evening.  She said that he then put his hand on her arm and said, “It would
be nice to get a bit more.”  She got out of the car quickly as she was
extremely uncomfortable.

[
51
]

On another
occasion, she was putting on her chef’s jacket at work and had not done up the
top button.  She said that Mr. Geluch looked down her shirt.  On other
occasions, Ms. Buell says that Mr. Geluch would go into the kitchen and engage
in sexual innuendos.  Once while she was preparing beef tenderloin, he said to
her “Is that the size you like?”  Ms. Buell testified that she ignored Mr.
Geluch but hated the comments.

[
52
]

Ms. Buell also said that Mr.
Geluch would shout at her and poke her on the shoulder and on the chest, while
berating her about rising food costs.  Following an incident in 1994, when she
left work to go to her son who was ill, she says that he called her in to
berate her.

[53]

b.

The
Law of Dismissal:

[78]

In
Reference Re
Public Service Employee Relations Act (Alta.)
,
1987 CanLII 88 (SCC)
,
[1987] 1 S.C.R. 313
at para.

91
,
38 D.L.R. (4
th
)
161
, Dickson C.J. wrote (in dissent), that:

Work is one of the most fundamental aspects in a
person’s life, providing the individual with a means of financial support and,
as importantly, a contributory role in society.  A person’s employment is an
essential component of his or her sense of identity, self-worth and emotional
well-being.

[79]

More recently, in
Wallace

v. United Grain Growers Ltd.
,
1997 CanLII 332 (SCC)
,
[1997] 3 S.C.R. 701
at para.
95
, the
Supreme Court of Canada also recognized that “the manner in which employment
can be terminated is equally important to an individual's identity as the work
itself.”

[80]

The “special relationship” and
the “unique characteristics” of the employment contract thus inform the law of
wrongful dismissal and the modern doctrine of just cause:
Wallace
,
supra

at para. 90.  As Justice Echlin and Matthew Certosimo explain in
Just Cause:
The Law of Summary Dismissal in Canada
(Aurora: Canada Law Book Inc., 2003)
at 1-3 (“
Just Cause
”), while the principles of contract law apply to the
employment context, “The power imbalance between employer and employee has been
said to differentiate employment contracts from ‘ordinary commercial contracts’”:
see
Wallace
,
supra
at paras. 91 and 92.  In
Ditchburn v.
Landis & Gyr Powers, Ltd.

(1995),
1995 CanLII 7290 (ON CTGD)
,
16 C.C.E.L. (2d) 1
at para.
2
(Ont.
Gen. Div.)
, varied on other grounds
(1997),
1997 CanLII 1500 (ON CA)
,
34 O.R. (3d) 578 (C.A.)
, the court
commented on the distinctiveness of the employment relationship, saying:

An employment relationship is based on contract.
However, it is not like purchasing a car – a contract governing a discrete
transaction.  It is a transitional contract in which each of the employer and
employee can reasonably expect more from each other as the relationship
continues.  As it is a contract governing a relationship between the parties,
almost by definition it continually changes.

[81]

At common law, an employer has
the right to dismiss an employee for misconduct, disobedience or incompetence,
or for a repudiatory breach of the employment contract.  As Echlin and
Certosimo explain at 2-4 of
Just Cause
, “A repudiation results from a
contracting party’s failure to perform a major obligation or set of obligations
in the contract, or failure to perform some obligation which has the ultimate
effect of depriving the other party of ‘substantially the whole benefit of the
contract’”: see
Hunter Engineering Co. v. Syncrude Canada Ltd.
,
1989 CanLII 129 (SCC)
,
[1989] 1 S.C.R. 426
,

57 D.L.R. (4
th
) 321
.  In the employment context, an employee may be
said to have repudiated the contract when, “The em`ployee’s conduct, and the
character it reveals, must be such as to undermine, or seriously impair, the
essential trust and confidence the employer is entitled to place in the
employee in the circumstances of their particular relationship”:
Ennis v.
Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce
(1986),
1986 CanLII 1208 (BC SC)
,
13 C.C.E.L. 25
at 27
(B.C.S.C.)
.  If the employer can establish that cause exists, no notice or
severance pay is required to terminate the employee.

[82]

The employer bears the onus of
demonstrating that cause exists for the employee’s discharge.  In Howard Levitt,

The Law of Dismissal in Canada
, 3
rd
ed. (Aurora: Canada Law
Book Inc., 2003) at 6-1, the author explained that: “The employer must prove
cause on the balance of probabilities, based on a finding of real incompetence
or misconduct, rather than simple dissatisfaction with performance or concern
as to potential misconduct.”  Levitt cautioned at 6-2, that: “Since dismissal
without notice is such a severe punishment, it can be justified only by
misconduct of the most serious kind.”  Indeed, Echlin and Certosimo, at 1-1 of
Just
Cause
, described an employee’s summary dismissal as the “capital
punishment” of the employment relationship.

[83]

There is no fixed rule of law
defining the degree of misconduct that justifies dismissal: see
Essery v.
John Lecky & Co.
(1986),
1986 CanLII 6434 (PE SCTD)
,
60 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 219 (P.E.I.S.C.)
.
In
R.
v. Arthurs
,
1967 CanLII 30 (ON CA)
,
[1967] 2 O.R. 49
at 55 (C.A.)
, rev’d
1968 CanLII 29 (SCC)
,
[1969] S.C.R. 85
,
Schroeder J.A. (in dissent) provided his definition as follows:

If an employee has been guilty of
serious misconduct, habitual neglect of duty, incompetence, or conduct
incompatible with his duties, or prejudicial to the employer’s business, or if
he has been guilty of wilful disobedience to the employer’s orders in a matter
of substance, the law recognizes the employer’s right summarily to dismiss the
delinquent employee.

[84]

To decide whether misconduct
constitutes just cause, a court must consider the nature of the misconduct and
the consequences arising from the misconduct, within the totality of the
employment context, including the nature and history of the employment
relationship.  In
McKinley v. BC Tel
,
2001 SCC 38 (CanLII)
,
[2001] 2 S.C.R. 161
at para.
57
,
the Supreme Court of Canada outlined the proper approach as being a
“contextual” one that:

examines
each case on its own particular facts and circumstances, and considers the
nature and seriousness of the dishonesty in order to assess whether it is
reconcilable with sustaining the employment relationship.  Such an approach
mitigates the possibility that an employee will be unduly punished by the
strict application of an unequivocal rule that equates all forms of dishonest
behaviour with just cause for dismissal.  At the same time, it would properly
emphasize that dishonesty going to the core of the employment relationship
carries the potential to warrant dismissal for just cause.

[85]

The test can thus be described
as involving two steps: first, the employer must establish the employee’s misconduct
on a balance of probabilities; second, the employer must establish that the
nature or degree of misconduct warranted dismissal.

i.

Establishing the Employee’s Misconduct:

[86]

There are many
types of employee misconduct that can be relied upon by an employer to justify
dismissal.  Furthermore, even if an individual item of conduct is insufficient
to warrant dismissal, the cumulative effect of numerous incidents of minor
misconduct may suffice: see
Ma v. Columbia Trust Co.
(1985),
1985 CanLII 686 (BC SC)
,
9 C.C.E.L. 300
at
para.
37
(B.C.S.C.).  The nature of the proof varies depending upon the type of
misconduct alleged.

1)

Theft, Fraud or Dishonesty:

[87]

Theft, fraud and dishonesty are likely the most
serious charges of misconduct justifying summary dismissal.  Even one isolated
act of theft is cause for dismissal: see
Ball v. MacMillan Bloedel Ltd.

(1989), 29 C.C.E.L. 99 (B.C.S.C.)
;
Kong v. Oshawa Group Ltd.

(1993), 46
C.C.E.L. 181 (Ont. Ct. Gen. Div.)
; and
Melanson v. Tandy Electronics Ltd.

(1987),
1987 CanLII 7819 (NB QB)
,
82 N.B.R. (2d) 181

(N.B.Q.B.(T.D.)).

[88]

A reasonably supported suspicion of theft may
justify dismissal:
Kong
,
supra
;
Leblanc v. Cartier
Co-operative Ltd.
(1980),
1980 CanLII 3144 (NB QB)
,
31 N.B.R. (2d) 284

(N.B.Q.B.(T.D.)); and
Wilson

v. Cornwall Publishing Co.
(1997),
1997 CanLII 3232 (BC SC)
,
32 C.C.E.L. (2d) 15

(B.C.S.C.).  The outcome of a criminal trial, in which theft must be proven
beyond a reasonable doubt, is irrelevant to the outcome of a wrongful dismissal
trial where an employer need only establish theft on the balance of
probabilities: see
Murphy v. Canadian Tire Corp.

(1991),
39 C.C.E.L. 205
(Ont.
Gen. Div.)
.  However, the onus on the employer to demonstrate that the
employee’s alleged dishonesty or theft justifies dismissal should be somewhat
higher than the usual civil standard of balance of probabilities, having regard
to the gravity of the consequences of proof of such a serious allegation: see
Homer
v. Roccha
(1988),
1988 CanLII 7489 (NB CA)
,
87 N.B.R. (2d) 277
, 20
C.C.E.L. 287 (N.B.C.A.);
Mackin v. Kings Regional Rehabilitation Centre

(1990),
1990 CanLII 4175 (NS SC)
,
95 N.S.R. (2d) 238

(N.S.S.C.(T.D.)).
For example, in
Havens v. John Watson Ltd.
,
[1999] B.C.J. No. 1201
(S.C.) (QL)
, var’d on another ground
[2000] B.C.J. No. 1178

(C.A.) (QL)
, when the plaintiff brought an action for wrongful dismissal, the
defendant glove manufacturing company counterclaimed, alleging theft after two
boxes of gloves went missing.  The court found for the plaintiff and held that
the defendant had failed to prove that the plaintiff had committed theft.  It
was noted, at para. 38, that employers would be put to strict proof of any
theft allegations due to the resulting stigma attached to the dishonesty in the
employment context.

[89]

Levitt stated at 6-41 of
The Law of Dismissal
in Canada
: “The general rule is that fraudulent activity by a senior
employee, even if done in good faith, is sufficient to justify the employee’s
dismissal.”  Again, the employer need only establish on a balance of
probabilities that the employee committed a fraudulent act.

[90]

As for whether an employee’s dishonesty
justifies summary dismissal, the leading case on this issue is the Supreme
Court of Canada’s decision in
McKinley
,
supra
.  In
McKinley
,

supra
at para.
48
,

Iacobucci J. stated on behalf of the court:

whether an employer is justified in dismissing an
employee on the grounds of dishonesty is a question that requires an assessment
of the context of the alleged misconduct. More specifically, the test is
whether the employee's dishonesty gave rise to a breakdown in the employment
relationship. This test can be expressed in different ways. One could say, for
example, that just cause for dismissal exists where the dishonesty violates an
essential condition of the employment contract, breaches the faith inherent to
the work relationship, or is fundamentally or directly inconsistent with the
employee's obligations to his or her employer.

[91]

While lesser sanctions may be applied to less
serious types of misconduct, Iacobucci J. acknowledged, at para. 51, that a
finding of “theft, misappropriation or serious fraud” would be a cause for
termination: see also
Christensen v. MacDougall
,
2001 CanLII 28309 (ON SC)
, [2001] O.T.C. 697, 14
C.C.E.L. (3d) 44 (Ont. Sup. Ct.).  In
Lane v. Canadian Depository for
Securities Ltd.

(1993),
49 C.C.E.L. 225
(Ont.
Gen. Div.)
, aff’d
1997 CanLII 14491 (ON CA)
,
29 C.C.E.L. (2d) 322

(C.A.), the plaintiff’s dishonesty as revealed by his misuse of credit
facilities, while it fell short of theft, was enough to justify his dismissal,
given his position of responsibility and the integrity expected of him: see
also
MacDonald v. Tamitik Status of Women Assn.
,
[1998] B.C.J. No. 2709

(S.C.) (QL)
.

(1)

Abusive Conduct:

[92]

Sexual harassment may be defined as “unwelcome
conduct of a sexual nature that detrimentally affects the work environment or
leads to adverse job-related consequences for the victims of the harassment”:
Janzen
v. Platy Enterprises Ltd.
,
1989 CanLII 97 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1252 at para.
56
. Like theft,
sexual harassment is a major offence, which may afford justification for
summary dismissal:
Neigum v. Wilike Co-operative Assn.
(1987),
1987 CanLII 4786 (SK QB)
,
55 Sask. R. 210
(Sask.
Q.B.);
Gonsalves v. Catholic Church Extension Society of Canada
,
supra
.

[93]

This reflects the fact that employers have a
duty to ensure that the work environment does not become so hostile,
embarrassing or otherwise so as to make continued employment intolerable:
Stamos
v. Annuity Research & Marketing Service Ltd.
,
[2002] O.T.C. 356
at
para. 62,
18 C.C.E.L. (3d) 117
(Sup.
Ct.)
.  In
Bannister v. General Motors of Canada Ltd.
(1998),
1998 CanLII 7151 (ON CA)
, 40 O.R.
(3d) 577, 164 D.L.R. (4
th
) 325 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal held that
an employer was justified in terminating a long-term employee in a supervisory
position on the grounds of sexual harassment.  While the trial judge had found
that the former supervisor was entitled to a warning, Carthy J.A. stated, at
para. 24, that, given the plaintiff’s status: “It was clearly an error of
omission to treat the respondent as if he was just one of many employees in the
department who may have joined with others in the improper conduct.”  As Carthy
J.A. continued, at para. 25:

…management ha[s] two positive duties: first, to members
of the workforce who are entitled to protection from offensive conduct and
second, to the corporation to protect it against civil suits at the hands of
individual complainants.

ii.

Establishing that Dismissal is Warranted:

[94]

The way that the employer treated the employee during the course
of the employment relationship and leading up to the dismissal, must be taken
into consideration.  “In practical terms,” say Echlin and Certosimo at 1-7 of
Just
Cause
, an employer’s chances of success at trial are “enhanced by evidence
of prior discipline or notice of dissatisfaction, such as in the context of a
poor performance evaluation or a negative decision respecting remuneration,
particularly for the same or similar misconduct”: see
United Electrical
Workers and Square D Co., Ltd. (Re)

(1955), 6 L.A.C. 289 (O.L.R.B.)
,
adopted in
Ritchie v. Intercontinental Packers Ltd.
(1982),

1982 CanLII 2538 (SK QB)
, 14
Sask. R. 206 at para.
9
, 2 C.C.E.L. 147 (Sask. Q.B.).

[95]

In some situations, employers have a duty to warn employees
about the consequences of continued misconduct, rather than dismiss them
summarily.  After surveying the case law in
The Law of Dismissal in Canada
,
Levitt concluded at 6-7, that: “Before an employee is terminated for cause, he
or she should be advised that the misconduct is a matter of serious
significance and its continuation could place his or her employment in
jeopardy”: see
Webb v. Eaton Yale Ltd.
,
[2003] O.J. No. 5013 at para. 43
(Sup. Ct.) (QL)
.  Of course, whether a prior warning and an opportunity to
improve must have been granted in order to justify summary dismissal depends on
the circumstances and the quality of the misconduct: “the greater the wrong,
the less likely it is that an employer will be required to first put the
employee on notice that such misconduct is not acceptable to the employer”: see

Leach v. Canadian Blood Services
,
2001 ABQB 54 (CanLII)
,
[2001] 5 W.W.R. 668
at
para.
117
, 7 C.C.E.L. (3d) 205 (Alta. Q.B.).

[96]

In
Fonceca v. McDonnell Douglas Canada Ltd.

(1983),
1 C.C.E.L. 51
at para.
16 (Ont. H.C.J.)
, the court held, “Where the incidents complained of are
trivial, but annoying, then warnings are necessary before termination for cause
is justified.  However, where incidents, each in themselves, are serious, even
though not sufficient to justify dismissal at the time, then a warning is not
essential”: see also
Atkinson v. Boyd, Phillips & Co.
(1979),
1979 CanLII 478 (BC CA)
, 9 B.C.L.R.
255 (C.A.).

[97]

In
Gonsalves v. Catholic Church Extension Society of Canada

(1998),
1998 CanLII 7152 (ON CA)
, 164 D.L.R. (4
th
) 339, 39 C.C.E.L. (2d) 104 (Ont. C.A.), a
long-term supervisory employee was accused of having made inappropriate sexual
comments, and two incidents of improper touching.  The court concluded that a
warning prior to dismissal was inappropriate, in part because of the
seriousness of the misconduct, together with the fact that he denied the
allegations.  However, an incident of sexual harassment may not always justify
summary dismissal.  In
MacDonald v. Valley Credits Ltd.
(1988), 13
A.C.W.S. (3d) 358 (B.C.S.C.)
, the court held that, for less serious instances
of sexual harassment, a warning that such misconduct may result in dismissal is
required before termination is justified.

[98]

Employers may also have an obligation to properly investigate
serious allegations, such as those of theft, fraud, or sexual harassment, to
provide the employee with an opportunity to respond to any such allegations,
prior to dismissing the employee: see
Francis v. Canadian Imperial Bank of
Commerce

(1992), 41 C.C.E.L. 37 at 48 (Ont. Gen. Div.)
, varied on other
grounds
1994 CanLII 1578 (ON CA)
, 21 O.R. (3d) 75 (C.A.).  In
Simpson v. Consumers’ Association of
Canada
(2001),
2001 CanLII 23994 (ON CA)
, 57 O.R. (3d) 351 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal reversed the
finding of the trial judge that a former Executive Director had been wrongfully
dismissed despite numerous incidents of inappropriate comments to and touching
of other employees.  However, at para. 90, Feldman J.A. noted that, “The respondent
had a fair opportunity to respond to the allegations.  This was a situation
where the CAC had no choice but to terminate [him].”

The implication is
that it was not only the allegations of sexual harassment, but also the fact
that the employer had given the employee a fair opportunity to respond, and
that his responses had been insufficient, which justified the dismissal.

[99]

Echlin and Certosimo also cautioned at 1-6 of
Just Cause
:
“where the employer has condoned similar misbehaviour in the past, a warning is
likely necessary to ‘lift the veil’ of condonation.”  If an employee’s
misconduct is known to the employer, and the employer does not terminate the
employee immediately, and instead provides the employee with commendation, a
salary increase, a letter of reference, etc. the employer may be found to have
condoned the misconduct.  The employer cannot thereafter rely on the misconduct
as a reason for dismissing the employee.

[100]

In
Murrell v. Burns International Security Services Ltd.
(1994),

1994 CanLII 7410 (ON CTGD)
,
5 C.C.E.L. (2d) 123

(Ont. Ct. Gen. Div.), the plaintiff was found to have been wrongfully dismissed
despite an allegation of sexual harassment.  The court held, at para. 34, that
the plaintiff’s dismissal could not be justified on those grounds, “as that
matter was investigated and dealt with.  Rivenbark did not find it a reason to
justify dismissal then and since there has been no repetition of the impugned
conduct, it cannot now be deemed to be cause for dismissal.”

[101]

Condonation should not, however, be assumed merely as a result of
a delay before termination.  The court in
Tracey v. Swansea Construction
,

1964 CanLII 271 (ON HCJ)
, [1965] 1 O.R. 203,
47 D.L.R. (2d) 295

(H.C.J.), aff’d
1965 CanLII 644 (ON CA)
, [1965] 2 O.R. 182, 50 D.L.R. (2d) 130 (C.A.), held that an
employer should be given a reasonable time to consider what action is
appropriate.  Furthermore, in
Fleming v. Safety Kleen Canada Inc.

(1996),
1996 CanLII 8138 (ON CTGD)
,
20 C.C.E.L. (2d) 140

at para.
29
(Ont. Gen. Div.), the court noted that some continued payment
following an employee’s misconduct can be interpreted as “an act of generosity
on the part of the company”: see also
Matheson v. Matheson International
Trucks Ltd.

(1984),
4 C.C.E.L. 271
at
para.7 (Ont. H.C.J.), where the court held that the defendant was not precluded
from alleging dismissal for cause merely because it had offered one month’s
severance pay to the plaintiff on his date of dismissal.  In
Connolly v.
General Motors of Canada Ltd.

(1993), 50 C.C.E.L. 247 at para. 42 (Ont.
Gen. Div.)
, the court summarized, “the cases establish that the court may
conclude that misconduct has been condoned where the court can draw such an
inference from all the circumstances, including any delay.”

[102]

Despite an employer’s duties to investigate allegations and to
warn employees prior to dismissal, as Echlin and Certosimo observe, at 1-6 of
Just
Cause
: “It has been a well-established rule at common law that an employer
does not have a duty to give reasons for dismissal at the time of dismissal,
nor does the employer have an obligation to grant the employee a hearing,
before making the decision to dismiss.”  One reason that employers do not have
a duty to give reasons at the time of dismissal, is that “an employer can rely
on an after-discovered ground as justifying or assisting to justify the initial
dismissal”:
Ma v. Columbia Trust Co.
,
supra
at para.
10
;
Lake
Ontario Portland Cement Co. v. Groner
,
1961 CanLII 1 (SCC)
,
[1961] S.C.R. 553
at
563, 28 D.L.R. (2d) 589.

[103]

However, while “allegations of cause, provided only after the
fact, can be relied on, the fact that they were not alleged at the time of
termination will affect their weight”: Levitt,
The Law of Dismissal in
Canada
,
supra
at 6-10.  This reflects an emerging duty of employers
“to be candid, reasonable, honest and forthright with their employees” at
dismissal: see
Wallace
,
supra

[104]

At para. 98.  As the court in
Boyes v. Saskatchewan Wheat Pool

(1982),
1982 CanLII 2639 (SK QB)
, 18 Sask. R. 361 at para.
16
(Q.B.) explained:

It is not
uncommon in a wrongful dismissal trial for the employer to dredge up every
incident arising during the term of employment which might tend to show the
employee in an unfavourable light, and the court must be diligent to
distinguish between those incidents which comprise the grounds for the
dismissal and those advanced for the sole purpose of discrediting the employee.

c.
Conclusion:

[105]

The essence of the employment relationship is that the employee
and employer are in an unequal bargaining relationship and that the employee is
in a vulnerable position.  In
Black v. Robinson Group Ltd
.,
[2002] O.T.C. 766

(Sup. Ct.)
, Pitt J. said, at para. 50, that, in wrongful dismissal cases, “The
courts are required to maintain the principle of proportionality between the
misconduct in question and the sanction imposed, and to avoid unduly
aggravating the power imbalance already inherent in the employment
relationship.”  In that case, the plaintiff had given herself unauthorized
salary increases and vacation pay.  However, Pitt J. described the misconduct,
at para. 37, as “indiscretion rather than dishonesty.”    The court adopted the
statement of Iacobucci J. in
McKinley
,
supra
at para.
54
:

Given [the]
recognition of the integral nature of work to the lives and identities of
individuals in our society, care must be taken in fashioning rules and
principles of law which would enable the employment relationship to be
terminated without notice. The importance of this is underscored by the power
imbalance that this Court has recognized as ingrained in most facets of the
employment relationship. In
Wallace
, both the majority and dissenting
opinions recognized that such relationships are typically characterized by
unequal bargaining power, which places employees in a vulnerable position
vis-à-vis their employers. It was further acknowledged that such vulnerability
remains in place, and becomes especially acute, at the time of dismissal.

[106]

Similarly, the court in
Varsity Plymouth Chrysler (1994) Ltd.
v. Pomerleau
(2002),
2002 ABQB 512 (CanLII)
,
5 Alta. L.R. (4th) 187

at para.
32
(Alta. Q.B.), held that to dismiss an employee who had fraudulently
reported personal-use purchase transactions, was disproportionate to the
misconduct, given that such practices were not unusual within the employer’s
particular business culture.

[107]

Adopting a contextual, fact-driven approach, I must analyze the
alleged reasons for which Mr. Geluch was dismissed, in order to determine
whether he committed acts that, either individually or in combination,
justified his dismissal.  According to the positions of the parties, these reasons
may have included: (i) fiscal impropriety, (ii) theft, (iii) abusive conduct,
and (iv) Mr. Geluch’s opposition to Rosedale’s membership application process.
In reaching my conclusion, I have given careful consideration to all the
evidence and to the totality of the employment relationship.

[108]

I also note that, in the year prior to his dismissal, Mr. Geluch
received a salary increase of $8,000.  In fact, throughout Mr. Geluch’s tenure
at Rosedale, he received salary increases.  There were never any formal
complaints filed against him.  Mr. Geluch was not given the nature of the
allegations made against him until February 1998 when his lawyer received
them.  At the time of his dismissal, Rosedale offered to allow Mr. Geluch to
resign publicly and kept him on the payroll for two months while counsel
discussed terms.  After two months, Rosedale stopped paying Mr. Geluch.
Rosedale never provided him with outplacement counselling and did not give him
a letter of reference.

i.
Fiscal
Impropriety:

[109]

Rosedale has alleged that Mr. Geluch acted improperly in having
the bookkeeper, Noreen Deely, write two cheques of $4,000 each, dated January
6, 1997.  This, says the Club, constituted an advance of salary for the 1997
year, despite the fact that, according to Rosedale’s policy manual, salaries
were to be paid bi-weekly and expenditures over $5,000 required a Director’s
signature.

[110]

I find that this incident occurred once, and once only.  Taking
the allowance early in the fiscal year without the knowledge of the Board was a
violation of Club policy. While Mr. Geluch says that he did this because Board
members were not available to sign a cheque of more than $5,000, it is
Rosedale’s position that Mr. Geluch did it this way so that subordinates who
reported to him could write the cheques.  No taxes were withheld. Mr. Geluch
made no efforts to conceal the salary advance.  It was noted in the books,
contained in his T-4 slip, and available for the auditors to review.  He agrees
that it may have been an error in judgment and that he opened himself up to
criticism by doing this.

[111]

At Rosedale, when cheques were written without a Director’s
signature, they would be initialled by the Finance
Committee Chair once they were returned.  They were also available to the
auditors each year for review.  Everything was properly recorded.

[112]

Mr. Geluch was entitled to a salary increase of $8,000 paid over
the course of the fiscal year.  He was under financial pressure because his son
was getting married.  However, while he was not deceptive in his actions, the
transaction was documented properly, and he paid income tax on the monies,
cheque-splitting and salary advances were in violation of Rosedale’s policies.
I accept that Mr. Geluch committed an error in judgment.  Since it never
happened before and did not happen again, I am of the view that his conduct
merited condemnation, but did not constitute conduct that amounted to cause for
immediate dismissal.

[113]

The second allegation of fiscal impropriety concerned Mr.
Geluch’s use of Rosedale’s credit card for personal expenses.  Mr. Geluch paid
for expenses at the Club by charging them to a TD Visa credit card in his name
or to an American Express credit card in Rosedale’s name.  The TD Visa
statements and certain supporting documentation for the years 1993 to 1997 were
produced in evidence at trial.  Business expenses included expenditures for:
food, wine, entertainment, and the rental and purchase of equipment and
supplies such as picture frames, lampshades, machinery, and newspapers.  Mr.
Geluch also used the TD Visa card for personal items.

[114]

It was Mr. Geluch’s practice to review the Visa statement each
month, mark those items that were personal by making certain notations on the
statement, and submit it to Violet Nettleton for payment.  Mr. Geluch would
provide a cheque, payable to Rosedale, for his personal expenses.  The cheque
would be noted in the general ledger account and posted to one of several
accounts, depending upon the particular expense in question.  On occasion, Mr.
Geluch made  repayment incrementally, and not at the time that the account was
due.

[115]

According to the auditor, Mr. Geluch did not have adequate
documentation to support the expenditures noted in the Visa statements.  In a
number of instances, he did not have the invoice from the vendor and did not
have the credit card receipt in order to properly document the business use.
He simply provided the Visa statement with notations made on it, and the amount
owing was paid to Visa by Rosedale. For the year 1997, less than twenty per cent
of the Visa statements had any supporting documentation.

[116]

The auditor categorized expenses by examining the supporting
documentation, looking at similar expenditures, reviewing the notation about
who may have been entertained, and by noting the nature, timing and location of
the purchase or expenditure.  On occasion, Mr. Geluch charged personal items
such as airfare and repaid Rosedale over time.  Certain of the expenses claimed
were for meals that the auditor categorized as “personal”, based upon the location
of the restaurants.  Examples given were Swiss Chalet in the west end of
Toronto, which was near Mr. Geluch’s house, Chez Piggy in Kingston, and Bert N’
Ernie’s, which was also in the west end and was not seen as the type of
establishment that would be used for entertaining for business purposes.  If
the location was not close to Rosedale and there was no clear business purpose
shown, the expenditure was classified as “personal”.

[117]

Similarly, purchases for liquor were expensed and no receipts
were submitted.  Mr. Geluch simply said that, as part of his job, he was
required to sample wines and to know about wines in order to improve the
quality of service at Rosedale.  That he made purchases at the LCBO was
surprising, since Rosedale has a licence to buy liquor and receives a five per
cent discount.  However, Mr. Geluch testified that the licence is very
restrictive and that is why he sometimes purchased liquor in stores.

[118]

On occasion, Mr. Geluch attended Club Managers’ conferences and
took holidays just before or after the educational program.  For example, in
February 1996, he took a vacation in Hawaii after attending the conference.  A
number of expenses were put on the credit card including airfare, meals and
accommodation.  Rosedale paid for all charges including certain personal
expenses, and Mr. Geluch reimbursed Rosedale with a cheque.  Rosedale issued
two cheques to avoid being over the $5,000 limit.  Mr. Geluch reimbursed
Rosedale, but did not pay the amount owing in full.  Rather he paid at the rate
of $500 per month.  In fact, following his dismissal, Mr. Geluch contacted
Violet Nettleton to say that he owed Rosedale monies for an airline ticket that
was a personal expense, and he paid that amount in January 1998.  He says that
he was very shaken by his dismissal and had forgotten about that account.

[119]

The evidence given by Mr. Geluch, which was not disputed by
Rosedale, was that he had an annual expense account of up to $3,000 to spend on
entertainment and meals.  While, initially, it was to be spent on the premises,
he was later told that he could spend it off-site.  During the twelve years of
his employment, no one told Mr. Geluch that they were unhappy with how he spent
the allowance.  No one from KPMG ever said that the method used for paying expenses
was problematic.  The location of a restaurant or a liquor store or the lack of
a receipt or other supportive documentation is not determinative of whether an
expense is for business or personal use.  Furthermore, in three examples
collated by Ms. MacDonald, LCBO purchases that were supported by documentation
had been categorized as “personal” expenses.

[120]

Unfortunately, there are no general ledger accounts for the years
1994 to 1997, with the exception of three, which were used for the review by
Ms. MacDonald.    Because the general ledgers were missing and not produced for
a number of the years in question, it was impossible to determine whether Mr.
Geluch had reimbursed the Club for certain personal expenses.  Without the
general ledger accounts it is not possible to say what payments were made for
wine, food and other expenses.

[121]

The practice of using the same credit card for personal and
business expenses went on for years.  All the information was available for the
auditor’s review and no mention was ever made about it.  The total amount
classified by the auditor as “personal” was $37,300.  In numerous examples put
to Ms. MacDonald in cross-examination, she admitted that she had made errors in
her assumptions and in her categorization of the expenses.  Frankly, in
considering the totality of her evidence, I am unable to place any weight upon
her report.  I am unable to see how Rosedale can rely on what it asserts were
personal expenses to justify dismissal.  While I accept that the personal use
of a business credit card is a bad business practice and that numerous credit
card charges, especially in 1997, were not supported by receipts, I am unable
to conclude that there was a breach of fiduciary duty by Mr. Geluch.  The use
of company funds for personal use has not been proven on a balance of
probabilities.

[122]

The third allegation of fiscal impropriety involved Mr. Geluch’s
claim that he was entitled to a clothing allowance.  Although it was not set
out in his letter of employment, Mr. Geluch testified that one of the terms of
his employment was that he had a clothing allowance, a taxable benefit to be
considered part of his annual salary.  He says that, some time during the year
1990-91, he spoke with Rosedale’s President Geoffrey Clarkson about the clothing
allowance and was told that if he did not exhaust the $2,000 annual allowance,
he could be paid the balance in cash.

[123]

Unfortunately, Mr. Clarkson, who was under subpoena, was
recovering from coronary by-pass surgery and was ordered by his doctor not to
give evidence at trial.  Mr. Geluch’s counsel agreed to excuse him for medical
reasons.

[124]

Mr. Geluch directed Violet Nettleton to set up his clothing
allowance by showing the expense in the general ledgers, and recording it at
the end of the year on his T4 slip.  When he did not spend the allowance, she
would give him a cheque for the balance owing.  It is Rosedale’s position that
the Board of Directors was unaware of this arrangement.  Rosedale says that Mr.
Geluch instructed staff to pay him an allowance on top of and not as part of
his salary, which was unauthorized.  Ms. Nettleton testified that she
understood that the clothing allowance was in addition to Mr. Geluch’s base
salary.  In four of five years, according to the summary made by Ms. MacDonald,
he exceeded the $2,000 amount.

[125]

The clothing allowance was reflected in the general ledger
accounts, which were reviewed by KPMG, Rosedale’s auditors, during the years
that Mr. Geluch was employed.  No one ever suggested that there was any
problem.  Since the evidence was that Anne Taylor and Kathleen Mannion each had
a clothing allowance, it is surprising that no reference was made to a clothing
allowance for Mr. Geluch.  If the Clubhouse Manager and the Catering Manager
had clothing allowances, it was likely that the General Manager would also have
one.  Mr. Geluch’s position was that the clothing allowance was paid in
addition to his salary; Rosedale disputes that such an allowance was approved.

[126]

It is difficult to resolve whether Mr. Geluch was paid more than
he was entitled for clothing.  Records submitted at trial suggest that no
clothing allowance was owing to Mr. Geluch.  However, each year the allowance
was claimed.    I find that, since all records were subject to scrutiny by
Rosedale’s auditors each year and no concerns were ever expressed, the
allegation concerning the clothing allowance cannot be considered just cause
for Mr. Geluch’s dismissal.  If the clothing allowance was part of his salary
rather than in addition to it, then the most that can be said is that Mr.
Geluch is indebted to Rosedale for the difference in what he was paid.

[127]

The final allegation involved Mr. Geluch’s conduct in his role as
Secretary/Treasurer of Rosedale.  During his employment, Mr. Geluch attended
every meeting of the Finance Committee, which reviewed financial statements
monthly and at year-end.  Rosedale changed auditors in 1996 and, when Ms.
MacDonald took over, she reviewed the prior audits and the earlier working
papers.  She noted that there were unadjusted differences which she felt should
have been made to the financial statements when they occurred. They involved,
for example, items such as bad debts, employer health tax and tax paid on
investment income by Rosedale.

[128]

Ms. MacDonald met with Mr. Geluch on December 20, 1996 to discuss
the audit for the year ending November 30, 1996.  She testified that, at the
time, they spoke about the adjustments that had been highlighted by KPMG, and
she had suggested to Mr. Geluch that the adjustments be put to the Finance
Committee, as there were liabilities from previous years that should be
recorded.  However, she says that Mr. Geluch told her that the Committee was
too busy to discuss the item because the agenda was full, and he said that he
would attend to that issue the following year.

[129]

Ms. MacDonald testified that she would normally have spoken
directly to the Finance Committee about this, but did not because Mr. Geluch
said that he would take care of it.  She claims that they met again to discuss
the issue in September or October 1997.  When Mr. Geluch was dismissed in late
October, she was conducting the annual audit and learned that the prior years’
adjustments had not been made.  The notice of the annual dues had already been
sent out to members when the Board learned about Rosedale’s true financial
position.  When the adjustments were made in the 1997 fiscal year, Rosedale
showed a deficit of over $400,000.  In the covering letter accompanying the
financial information sent out to Club members, the President was critical of
the performance of senior management.

[130]

Mr. Geluch denies that he was ever told of Ms. MacDonald’s desire
to speak to the Finance Committee or that he should make the financial
adjustments.

[131]

I find that Ms. MacDonald did have conversations with Mr. Geluch
on December 20, 1996 and in October 1997, and that she mentioned that
adjustments had to be made to the financial statements.  I am also mindful that
Mr. Geluch was a fiduciary and owed duties to Rosedale.  However, the totality
of the evidence on these audit adjustments does not amount to financial
mismanagement and grounds for dismissal.

[132]

Clearly, it is good practice for adjustments to be made annually
rather than to allow them to accumulate.  By not booking those entries in a
timely way, the impact of these non-recurring costs was not noted.  By the time
they were entered, they related to prior years, but had a significant impact on
the balance sheet.  However, there is no suggestion that KPMG ever had anything
on file directing Mr. Geluch to make the unadjusted entries, or that he failed
to do so.  When Rosedale’s new accountant, Ms. MacDonald, came on the scene,
she may have felt differently but she did not, in my view, emphasize the
importance of timely adjustments in her advice to Mr. Geluch.  In fact, she admitted
in her testimony that, in her view, the adjustments were not “material”.

[133]

It may have been desirable for Mr. Geluch to have entries made in
a timely way, but it was not mandatory.  Certainly, the failure to make timely
adjustments that were not material, would not form the basis of grounds for
immediate dismissal.  In my view, it was convenient to blame Mr. Geluch for
unadjusted entries and allege “mismanagement” following his dismissal.

ii.
Theft:

[134]

Rosedale has also made several allegations of theft or wrongful
appropriation against Mr. Geluch.  The first allegation involved appropriation
of Rosedale’s property.  Ross Irwin, the Club maintenance supervisor, gave
evidence that Mr. Geluch had requested that he build a ski rack and a kitchen
table for his house, that he saw flower boxes which he had built for Rosedale
at Mr. Geluch’s house, and that Mr. Geluch had asked him to refinish an antique
table and to remove a car radio while he was at work.  Mr. Geluch denies the
allegations and says that he paid for the kitchen table.

[135]

During cross-examination, Mr. Irwin was shown to have a poor
memory and did not recollect where Mr. Geluch lived.  Frankly, from the
evidence led, I am not at all certain where the extra flower boxes found
themselves.  However, I accept Mr. Irwin’s evidence that he built a ski rack, a
kitchen table and finished an antique table for Mr. Geluch.  I also find that
he helped Mr. Geluch remove a radio from his car.  Mr. Irwin built a number of
items of furniture for Rosedale and for some of the senior staff.  If it was
for personal use, and involved the use of Club property or happened during
working hours, then Mr. Geluch owes Rosedale something.

[136]

The issue is whether this conduct amounts to sufficient cause for
immediate dismissal.  In my view, these practices were undesirable, but not so
significant as to justify dismissal.

[137]

The second allegation involves the supposed appropriation of food
and wine from Rosedale for Mr. Geluch’s private use.  Mr. Geluch testified that
he would often work a long day and would eat his meals at Rosedale.  Sometimes,
he took prepared food home for himself.  He said that if he took food home for
others, he would note it and pay for it.  It was Ms. Mannion’s understanding
that one of the privileges that Mr. Geluch enjoyed was that he could test any
food he wanted and that, since he worked long days, he could take a meal home
with him.  There was no suggestion that Mr. Geluch was abusing the food
privileges.  Michael Romano also confirmed that Mr. Geluch worked long hours
and that it was the practice for general managers to eat in the Club’s
restaurant and to take food home.  It was also common practice to taste food
and wine.  One of the responsibilities in providing hospitality was to ensure
that quality was achieved.  Therefore, it was also appropriate that Mr. Geluch
take wine home to taste.

[138]

Staff members were entitled to take wine but were required to
fill out a chit and have it noted in the Staff Purchases Journal.  All wine and
liquor purchases were recorded in a journal that was kept in the liquor room
for inventory purposes.  Payments would be posted in the cash receipt journal.
According to these records, Violet Nettleton took wine home on a regular basis
four or five times a month and did not repay the Club.

[139]

At trial, the only evidence about practices in private clubs
concerning food was the evidence led by the plaintiff.  Where a manager spends
a great deal of time at work, the practice seems to be to allow the manager to
consume food for his own use.  I am not satisfied that Mr. Geluch took
advantage of this practice to the detriment of Rosedale.  Furthermore, the
evidence is not persuasive that he took wine for his own personal use.  Rather,
the evidence before me that I would consider to be reliable is that Mr. Geluch
paid for any wine that he took for his personal use and that it was part of his
job to sample wines and to entertain others in order to enhance the quality of
food and beverage at Rosedale.  As the complete package of general ledgers are
unavailable, it is impossible to determine whether Mr. Geluch breached the
terms of his employment by personal consumption of food and wine.  For that
reason too, the assertion that this allegation constitutes just cause has not
been proven on a balance of probabilities.

iii.

Abusive Conduct:

[140]

After their meeting with Ms. Taylor, Mr. Newbould and Mr. Cowie
reported to the Board at an emergency meeting and the Board voted to dismiss
Mr. Geluch immediately.  Rosedale did not follow its own sexual harassment
policy, which required management to interview the complainant, the person
alleged to have harassed the staff member, and any relevant witnesses.  Mr.
Newbould testified that the reason the protocol was not followed was that Anne
Taylor was reluctant to proceed and that she and Melva Buell did not file a
“complaint”.  Mr. Newbould also testified that the reason for not conducting a
full investigation, which would have involved interviewing Mr. Geluch, was a
concern that he would engage in reprisal conduct with the staff.  He also
testified that the reason that Mr. Geluch was not given specific grounds for
his dismissal was that Rosedale had undertaken to Anne Taylor that they would
not disclose that she was the source of the complaints.

[141]

Mr. Geluch took his job as General Manager seriously and
dedicated himself to his work.  In attempting to raise the standards at
Rosedale, he imposed pressure on staff to work harder and to offer higher
quality service.  At times, when he was under pressure, he would challenge his
staff about rising costs, service issues and job performance.  His conduct
would consist of shouting, swearing, using threatening words and closing in on
personal space.  He was described as being very tactile and would become
physical by poking a staff member on the shoulder in order to prove a point.
His style was described as “volatile”.  Whenever food costs were an issue,
there would be a shouting match.  He was not sympathetic to staff who were
absent from work, such as Ms. Buell, who took time off because of her son, or
Mr. Irwin, who was off work because of his medical condition.  This
unsympathetic reaction was not frequent, but when it occurred it was difficult
for staff to handle.  An employer should not have to resort to such behaviour
in order to effect results.  Some of the staff were not subjected to this
behaviour and described Mr. Geluch as a wonderful boss.

[142]

The allegations by Anne Taylor concerned incidents that were
alleged to have occurred in May 1989, December 1989 and December 1992.  None of
the incidents were raised with Mr. Geluch at the time.  When they were
described to Mr. Newbould in 1997, Mr. Geluch was not given an opportunity to
respond.  The reason given for this was that Rosedale Board members believed
that they needed to protect their staff.  There was concern that there would be
repercussions for staff if the allegations were disclosed.  This was the same
reason why Rosedale voted to dismiss Mr. Geluch, rather than to suspend him
temporarily.  Mr. Newbould had an agreement with Anne Taylor not to disclose
what she had said without her consent, and that, if she lost her job, Rosedale
would indemnify her.

[143]

Mr. Newbould stated in his testimony that the allegations by Anne
Taylor were the sole reason for Mr. Geluch’s dismissal.  Another Board member,
Anne Carter, confirmed that was the case.  She was dismayed that Anne Taylor,
whom she considered to be an outstanding employee, had left because she had
been treated shabbily at Rosedale.  Mr. Findlay testified that, at the
emergency meeting of the Board, the members discussed what Ms. Taylor had said,
that she had been poked in the shoulder, that she was subjected to a sexual
comment, that staff were frequently reduced to tears, and that she had seen Mr.
Geluch take items home from the wine cellar.

[144]

The members of the Board of Directors voted to dismiss Mr. Geluch
immediately and without notice.  According to those who testified, they were
very concerned about the treatment that Anne Taylor had received and they acted
as soon as they became aware of it.

[145]

Rosedale relies on other allegations as well.  Board member Paul
Findlay described the environment at Rosedale as a “poisoned” environment based
upon what he had been told by Mr. Newbould and Mr. Cowie.  The Board accepted
what Ms. Taylor said, believed that she had no reason to make up the
allegations, and it did not see any value in receiving Mr. Geluch’s response.

[146]

In my view, the defence witnesses who described Mr. Geluch’s
conduct were credible.  So too were the witnesses, Mr. Westaway and Mr. Romano,
called by the plaintiff.  Their evidence is not really contradictory.  Mr.
Geluch was a hardworking professional who imposed his work ethic on his staff.
When he was feeling pressured about issues such as rising food costs, he took
it out on them.  Whether such actions amount to abuse of staff is the issue.

[147]

As for the incidents of sexual harassment involving Melva Buell,
they are alleged to have occurred in 1992.  Certainly, Mr. Geluch’s conduct, as
described by her, made Ms. Buell feel uncomfortable and uneasy.  She did not
relate any incidents involving sexual harassment to have occurred at any time
after that date; Ms. Buell never filed any complaints.  There was no evidence
led to suggest that Ms. Buell was treated negatively (that is, that she did not
receive promotions or salary increases).  In cases alleging sexual harassment,
the court must consider the effect of the conduct on the victim.  In this case,
Ms. Buell continued working at Rosedale until 1996 and left to open a business.
While she considered Mr. Geluch’s comments to be offensive when they involved
sexual innuendo, she never asked him to stop speaking that way.

[148]

Rosedale did not follow its own sexual harassment policy for the
conduct of an investigation.  Applying the contextual approach, I am not
satisfied that the defendant has met its burden to demonstrate that there was
ongoing conduct amounting to abuse.  The incidents were sporadic and did not
amount to what would be considered systematic abuse of a nature that is described
in the case law and would justify dismissal.

[149]

Certainly, when Mr. Geluch was under pressure as a result of
rising food costs, he challenged Ms. Buell and they exchanged words.  Speaking
in a loud voice and berating a staff member is not suitable conduct for a
person in a supervisory position.  However, such conduct may not constitute
just cause for immediate dismissal in every case.  Rather, it is a proper
subject for a warning to an employee in most instances.

[150]

Similarly, poking a staff member on the shoulder is technically
physical assault.  In the case of Ms. Taylor, it occurred along with scolding.
In my view, that conduct is unacceptable in the workplace and is deserving of a
warning, but, again, taken in its context, it does not constitute just cause
for dismissal.

[151]

In order to conduct performance reviews and to address the
question of salary increases, it became the custom that Rosedale’s Executive
Committee would meet on a Saturday morning prior to the year-end.  At that
time, Mr. Geluch would present proposals for salary increases for senior
staff.  He would also be advised of his salary increase.  In 1996, Mr. Geluch
received a letter dated November 18, 1996, which recorded the ratings and
salary increases of senior staff.  In that letter, Mr. Geluch wrote down his
own ratings, as they were provided orally by the Executive Committee:

1.

Staff
management: A to A-

2.

Public
Image: A+

3.

Budget
and Finance: B+ to A

4.

Member
relations: B

[152]

Mr. Geluch was given a salary increase of $8,000 for the 1997 year.
At the time that he was dismissed, he was earning a little more than $129,000
and had a car allowance of $8,000.  He had received regular annual increases
from the date he was hired.  There had never been a complaint filed by any
staff member about his conduct.  He was never warned by Rosedale about any
problems with the staff or members.

[153]

In reviewing each of the allegations made against Mr. Geluch
that Rosedale submits constitute sufficient cause for his summary dismissal, I
have reached the conclusion that the incidents alleged do not constitute just
cause, neither individually nor cumulatively.  The defendant has the onus of
proving cause on a balance of probabilities and I am not satisfied that the
burden has been met.  Applying a contextual approach, I cannot say that the
defence has established that a breach of fiduciary obligations took place.
While the cumulative effect of a series of incidents can amount to cause, I am
unable to conclude that these incidents are of such a nature.  No doubt, Mr.
Geluch was to be a role model for other employees; however, it cannot be said
that he breached his obligation to serve the organization.

[154]

In my opinion, what happened in this case is that, over the
twelve years of his employment at Rosedale, Mr. Geluch did a number of things
that caused certain prominent members to lose confidence in his ability.  In
essence, he failed to keep the Board members happy.  That is evident even from
his performance review in 1996 when the evaluation of his abilities in “Member
relations” was considered a “B”, as compared with higher marks in other areas.
When the circumstances of Anne Taylor’s departure became known to the Board,
