the Board decided that there was a “poisoned environment” under Mr. Geluch’s
leadership, and determined that he should be fired immediately.

[155]

Clearly, certain of the staff enjoyed working under Mr. Geluch’s
direction and described him as a great General Manager and a great boss.
Others were not so enamoured with his style.  He was difficult when he was
under pressure and he took out his problems on his staff.  On occasion, they
were brought to tears.  Some former members of Rosedale attested to Mr.
Geluch’s accomplishments in terms of the improved quality of the golf course,
the food and beverage.  Obviously, others did not support the continuation of
his position.

[156]

I find that the Board members were misguided in their approach.
When the Board learned about the allegations of Anne Taylor, it should have
directed that an independent person be retained to investigate the matter
fully.  Instead, the Board chose to protect a former employee rather than
confront its senior executive and afford him an opportunity to respond.  Mr.
Geluch should have been suspended with pay pending a full investigation and given
an opportunity to respond to the allegations.  Rosedale’s explanation that
staff were afraid of Mr. Geluch and would not come forward had he been
suspended, was convenient, but simply not borne out in the evidence.  The
information collected should have been presented to the Board for their
impartial determination.

[157]

In a workplace investigation, procedural safeguards must be put
in place.  This is particularly so where there is a sexual harassment policy
that sets out a procedure for investigating complaints.  Although neither Anne
Taylor nor Melva Buell had filed a formal complaint, their allegations were
treated like complaints and were used as the basis of dismissal.  Mr. Geluch,
as a long-serving employee, was not treated fairly by his employer and was not
afforded any opportunity to tell his side of the story or to respond in any
way.

[158]

In reaching these conclusions, I take into account the evidence
led by the defence concerning the allegations of cause and the position of the
plaintiff.  There are numerous inconsistencies in the plaintiff’s evidence,
and, as revealed in cross-examination, between his evidence at trial and the
evidence he provided upon his examination for discovery.  However, while there
are numerous inconsistencies which affect the strength of his evidence, they
are on peripheral issues and do not bear upon the essence of the case.

[159]

Given that allegations made by Rosedale do not constitute just
cause for immediate dismissal, either individually or collectively, I find that
Mr. Geluch was wrongfully dismissed.  It is particularly significant that he
had never received warnings about inappropriate behaviour in the past and that
there was no record in his personnel file of any disciplinary action taken
against him before his dismissal on October 31, 1997.

iv.
Opposition to the Membership Application Process
:

[160]

Rosedale took the position that this case has nothing to do with
individual applications for membership or with the application process at
Rosedale in general.  When the Board discussed Mr. Geluch’s employment and
voted to dismiss him immediately, the Directors did not discuss anything about
membership applications. Mr. Geluch, however, believes that, because he was
outspoken about the discriminatory membership policies in 1996, certain Board
members were angry with him at the time, and that they later voted to dismiss
him summarily.

[161]

The evidence was that Rosedale had a membership application
process that was being revised in 1996.  The Board passed certain changes to
the by-laws which were approved by the general membership in 1997, eliminating
the “blackball system” in order to prevent arbitrary voting.  The changes were
set out in an Information Circular and Amendment of Bylaw passed at the
February 12, 1997 annual meeting.  The new system, which was set out in the
consolidated copy of the Bylaws dated March 16, 1998, was that those interested
in applying for membership would have their names circulated among the
membership, comments would be solicited and if 80% or more voted in favour of the
applicant, then the application would be sent to the Board.  If the Board voted
in favour of the applicant, the membership would be approved.

[162]

George and Susan Cohon applied for membership at Rosedale in
1996.  Their applications were deferred and re-submitted in 1997, once the
changes in the policies had been made.  Both applications were approved in
1997.  Mr. Newbould, who was on the Board at the time, but not on the
Membership Committee, said that the issue of Mr. Cohon being Jewish was raised
and discussed by the Board, as Mr. Cohon was a prominent member of the Jewish
community.

[163]

Mr. Geluch testified that he was outspoken about the rejection of
Mr. Cohon’s application and about the unfairness of the process to the
Membership Committee.  He believes that certain Board members were not pleased
with his position.  Rosedale took the position that Mr. Geluch did not have a
vote on membership matters and that he expressed no opinions about the
process.  Furthermore, Mr. Findlay testified that he was a Board member at the
time that Mr. Cohon’s application was approved by the Membership Committee in
July 1997, and that it was approved unanimously by the Board.  Rosedale submits
that any allegation of discriminatory practice and, in particular,
anti-Semitism, was unfounded.

[164]

I find that Mr. Geluch was searching for reasons why he was
dismissed and, therefore, he claimed that his position regarding the membership
application process was a possible cause.  Because Rosedale did not provide Mr.
Geluch with any explanation for firing him, he was forced to speculate.  I find
that, while Rosedale had policies in place prior to 1997 that allowed for
arbitrary voting which may in turn have promoted discriminatory practices,
Rosedale’s membership decided to revise their application process.  New
provisions were discussed in 1996 and effected in 1997.

[165]

The policies of a private social club are matters for the
membership rather than for the courts to decide, unless the organization
provides a service to the public.  The membership policies that were in
existence at Rosedale until recently were arbitrary, potentially
discriminating, and offensive in a modern, civilized society.  However, I find
that discussions about Mr. Cohon’s application for membership had nothing to do
with Mr. Geluch’s dismissal from Rosedale.

[166]

Frankly, while I agree with Rosedale that these allegations about
membership policies were not relevant to the matter before this court, I was
not given any explanation as to why, when such allegations were front and centre
in the statement of claim, the defendant did not take steps through pre-trial
procedures to seek to strike out portions of the claim.

VI.

IF MR. GELUCH WAS WRONGFULLY DISMISSED, WHAT IS THE APPROPRIATE
PERIOD OF NOTICE?

a.
The Test for Determining Reasonable Notice:

[167]

In
The Law of Dismissal in Canada
, Levitt states at 8-2,
that: “In the absence of a contract for a definite period of employment, the
law presumes an indefinite hiring subject to termination on reasonable
notice.”  Traditionally, if reasonable notice is not given, the employer must
compensate the employee by an award of damages that is intended to place the
employee in the position in which he would have been had he received proper
notice:
Ansari v. British Columbia Hydro and Power Authority
(1986),
1986 CanLII 1023 (BC SC)
, 2
B.C.L.R. (2d) 33 at 36 (S.C.), aff’d
[1986] B.C.J. No. 3006

(C.A.) (QL)
.  While there is no fixed formula for determining reasonable
notice, in the majority of cases, the courts have approved a more fact-based,
contextual approach, as was enunciated by the court in
Bardal v. Globe and
Mail Ltd.
(1960),
1960 CanLII 294 (ON HCJ)
, 24 D.L.R. (2d) 140 at 144-5 (Ont. H.C.J.).  In
Bardal
,
McRuer C.J.H.C. stated, at 145:

There can be no
catalogue laid down as to what is reasonable notice in particular classes of
cases.  The reasonableness of the notice must be decided with reference to each
particular case, having regard to the character of the employment, the length
of service of the servant, the age of the servant and the availability of
similar employment, having regard to the experience, training and
qualifications of the servant.

[168]

The Supreme Court adopted this passage in
Wallace
,
supra
.
As is evident from
Bardal
,
supra
, there are almost as many
factors that can be considered in determining reasonable notice as there are
cases that have raised the issue.  However, a few specific factors have been
emphasized repeatedly by the courts.  In
Anderson v. Haakon Industries
(Canada) Ltd.
(1987),
1987 CanLII 2406 (BC CA)
,
23 B.C.L.R. (2d) 166
,
48
D.L.R. (4th) 235
(C.A.), the British Columbia Court of Appeal upheld a
trial judge’s decision to award a former General Manager sixteen months’ notice
in a wrongful dismissal action.  The trial judge had found that the plaintiff
had been dismissed from his employment without notice, in breach of the
contract of employment.  In calculating the reasonable notice period, the trial
judge considered four factors to be of major importance: (1) the age of the employee,
(2) the employee’s length of service, (3) the character of the employment, and
(4) the availability of similar employment.  The Court of Appeal held that
these were the proper factors to consider.

[169]

The same four factors, age, length of service, the responsibility
of the employment function, and the availability of equivalent alternative
employment, were also emphasized by McEachern C.J.S.C. in
Ansari
,
supra

at 43, although he also recognized that what is objectively reasonable depends
upon the circumstances of each case.  Similarly, in
Boyd v. Whistler
Mountain Ski Corp.
,
[1990] B.C.J. No. 821 (S.C.) (QL)
, the trial judge
emphasized the same four factors as being particularly important in fixing the
requisite notice period for a 55 year-old former Vice President at 15 months.
Other such cases include:
MacLean v. Audiovox Corp.
(1994),
1994 CanLII 2090 (BC CA)
,
99 B.C.L.R. (2d) 383
,
8 C.C.E.L. (2d) 24

(C.A.) (a 62 year-old was awarded 20 months’ notice, after holding a very
responsible position for 15 years),
Lyle v. Aluminex Extrusions Ltd.

(1996),
17 C.C.E.L. (2d) 320

(B.C.S.C.)
(a 56 year-old former Director and General Manager was awarded 20
months’ notice, after his dismissal after 15 years of service),
Gilbert v.
Wittnauer Worldwide L.P.
(2002),
2002 CanLII 45073 (ON CA)
,
23 C.C.E.L. (3d) 35

(C.A.) (a former Vice President of sales was given 18 months’ notice following
13 years of service), and
Kidd v. Hudson’s Bay Co.
,
[2003] O.T.C. 335
,
25 C.C.E.L., (3d) 102

(Sup. Ct.)
(a 47 year-old former industrial engineering manager was awarded 18
months notice following 17 years of service).

b.
Conclusion:

[170]

Mr. Geluch claims that he was entitled to a notice period of
fifteen to eighteen months, given his age (fifty-four years old), his position
of employment (General Manager), the length of his years of service (twelve years),
and the level of his salary (approximately $129,000 at the time of his
dismissal).  He also pointed out that the Office Manager, Violet Nettleton,
received fifteen months as severance pay when she was required to take early
retirement.

[171]

Rosedale’s position is that the cause allegations were reasonable
and
bona fide
, and that they treated Mr. Geluch fairly by doing the
following:

1.

they
gave him the option of resigning in order to avoid being dismissed;

2.

they
did not tell members the reasons for his dismissal and merely said that he had
left Rosedale; and

3.

they
provided him with salary and benefits for two months pending resolution of the
dispute.

[172]

Mr. Geluch testified that he sent out over seventy letters of
application all over the world, but had difficulty securing employment.  He
found it especially difficult in the Toronto area as there was “a cloud of
questions” whenever he was asked about his dismissal and he could not answer
but to say that he was involved in litigation.  The private club industry is small
and word spread.  He found the situation awkward.  After thirteen months, he
found employment as General Manager at the Seymour Golf and Country Club in
Vancouver.

[173]

In considering the circumstances surrounding Mr. Geluch’s
dismissal from Rosedale, I find that he was dismissed summarily without warning
and without explanation.  He was never given an opportunity to respond to the
allegations made against him.  The Board had relied upon what it had been told
and had acted with haste.  They offered to allow him to resign and gave him
only a few minutes to make that decision.  He was escorted out the door in the
presence of other staff members.

[174]

In circumstances such as these, Rosedale could have suspended Mr.
Geluch for a period of time while an investigation was undertaken, and allowed
him the opportunity to address the allegations that were made.  Rosedale chose
not to do so.

[175]

Thus, the notice period to which Mr. Geluch is reasonably
entitled is 15 months.  In that he was able to secure employment after reasonable
efforts within 13 months, the monies he earned during the period of notice are
deducted.

VII.

IS MR. GELUCH ENTITLED TO ADDITIONAL
DAMAGES?

[176]

In
Vorvis v. Insurance Corporation of British Columbia
,

1989 CanLII 93 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1085, 58 D.L.R. (4
th
) 193, the Supreme Court of
Canada made it clear that the award of aggravated or punitive damages will be
rare in cases of contract law.  In
Wallace
,
supra
,

it
emphasized that the conduct giving rise to either type of damage must be a
separate actionable wrong.

a.
The
Claim for Wallace Damages:

[177]

Another factor that affects the amount of notice to be awarded,
is the manner of dismissal.  In
Rahemtulla v. Vanfed Credit Union
,
1984 CanLII 689 (BC SC)
,
[1984] 3 W.W.R. 296
at
para.
32
,
51 B.C.L.R. 200
(S.C.), McLachlin
J., as she then was, said:

The employer,
having decided to terminate the plaintiff, had two choices open to
it.  It could terminate her in the usual course, in a fashion which
cast no moral cloud upon her character.  Or it could terminate her
for cause as it did, leaving her with a stigma which would make it much more
difficult to find new employment. Having chosen the latter course, and having
failed to substantiate the cause, the employer must be held responsible for the
longer period of unemployment to which its unjustified conduct contributed.

[178]

The Supreme Court expanded this approach in
Wallace
,
supra
,
and it has since become known as the “
Wallace
factor”.  In
Wallace
,
while the entire court agreed that if an employer dismisses an employee in a
manner that makes it more difficult for that employee to obtain alternate
employment then the notice period will be increased, the majority of the court
also held that the notice period could be increased if the employer, in
dismissing the employee, was particularly insensitive.  Iacobbuci J. explained,
at para. 88:

The appellant urged this Court to recognize the
ability of a dismissed employee to sue in contract or alternatively in tort for
“bad faith discharge”. Although I have rejected both as avenues for recovery,
by no means do I condone the behaviour of employers who subject employees to
callous and insensitive treatment in their dismissal, showing no regard for
their welfare. Rather, I believe that such bad faith conduct in the manner of
dismissal is another factor that is properly compensated for by an addition to
the notice period.

…

The obligation
of good faith and fair dealing is incapable of precise definition.  However, at
a minimum, I believe that in the course of dismissal employers ought to be
candid, reasonable, honest and forthright with their employees and should
refrain from engaging in conduct that is unfair or is in bad faith by being,
for example, untruthful, misleading or unduly insensitive.

[179]

This reasoning was adopted by the court in
Deildal v. Tod
Mountain Development Ltd.
(1995),
1995 CanLII 567 (BC SC)
,
10 C.C.E.L. (2d) 202

(B.C.S.C.), aff’d
1997 CanLII 4076 (BC CA)
,
[1997] 6 W.W.R. 239

(C.A.), leave to appeal dismissed (without reasons) by the Supreme Court,
[1997] S.C.C.A. No. 338
.
In
Deildal
, a 50 year-old former General Manager was awarded 15 months’
notice, after being wrongfully dismissed following 10 years of service.  In
addition, the court held that since the plaintiff would have great difficulty
finding appropriate or equivalent work in his field as a result of the
defendant’s assertions of theft, dishonesty and incompetence, the equivalent of
12 months’ salary would be added to the plaintiff’s award of damages.  Finally,
6 months were added as aggravated damages, to compensate the plaintiff for
mental distress.  The court said, at paras. 64-65:

It is clear that
one of the factors to consider when assessing the length of the notice period
is the degree of difficulty which the employee will encounter when attempting
to find another position.  While it may be that in a “clean firing”
the plaintiff is not entitled to extra time or damages simply because of the
fact that he was fired, I am not satisfied that such is the case where
groundless, slanderous accusations of incompetence and dishonesty are made at
the time of termination and thereafter.  It seems to me that in such
circumstances it may be said, that at the time the contract of employment was
entered into it was in the contemplation of both parties that if at the time of
termination the plaintiff was wrongfully accused of incompetence and
dishonesty, and this was made known to others in the social and work
communities, that the plaintiff would require more time to find comparable
employment, then would have been ordinarily within their
contemplation.  It seems to me further that at the time the
accusations were made, and subsequently repeated, it was clearly foreseeable,
and within the contemplation of the parties, that mental distress would
probably follow.

[180]

In
Black v. Robinson Group Ltd.
,
supra
, a 61
year-old accountant was awarded 12 months’ notice after being wrongfully dismissed
following 12 years of service.  However, since the employer had also unlawfully
withheld three weeks pay upon termination, the plaintiff was given an
additional 2 months’ notice as additional damages.  Other similar cases
include:
Cassady v. Wyeth-Ayerst Canada Inc.
(1998),
1998 CanLII 6509 (BC CA)
,
163 D.L.R. (4th) 1
,
54 B.C.L.R. (3d) 68

(C.A.) (the appellate court added $10,000 to a $30,000 notice award to a former
sales representative who had been dismissed after four years of service, on the
basis of the employer’s bad faith conduct regarding the dismissal had adverse
consequences for the plaintiff);
Noseworthy v. Riverside Pontiac-Buick Ltd.

(1998),
1998 CanLII 2751 (ON CA)
,
168 D.L.R. (4th) 629
,
39 C.C.E.L. (2d) 37

(C.A.), (where the plaintiff suffered from traumatic stress disorder as a
result of his abrupt termination and his employer’s allegations of forgery, the
appellate court considered 10 months to be an appropriate period of reasonable
notice);
Kissner v. Goodall & Hills

(1999),
102 O.T.C. 210
(Sup.
Ct.)
(the court awarded three additional months of notice as a result of the
employer’s bad faith manner of dismissal);
Antonacci v. Great Atlantic &
Pacific Co. of Canada
(1998),
1998 CanLII 14734 (ON CTGD)
,
53 O.T.C. 291
,
35 C.C.E.L. (2d) 1

(Ont. Gen. Div.), aff’d
2000 CanLII 26963 (ON CA)
,
49 C.C.E.L. (2d) 122

(C.A.),  var’d on other grounds
2000 CanLII 5496 (ON CA)
,
128 O.A.C. 236
(C.A.)
(the employer’s serious and unfounded allegations of poor performance justified
an extension of the notice period to 24 months);
Marshall v. Watson Wyatt
& Co.
(2002),
2002 CanLII 13354 (ON CA)
, 57 O.R. (3d) 813 (C.A.) (the employer’s breach of its
obligation of “good faith and fair dealing” led to a three-month extension of
the notice period); and
Zorn-Smith v. Bank of Montreal
,
[2003] O.J. No.
5044 (Sup. Ct.) (QL)
(the employer’s bad faith and unfair dealing justified a
longer notice period).

[181]

In Loreta Zubas & Anusha Alikhan, “Where’s Wallace?
Searching for an understanding of recent Wallace awards!” (Paper presented to
the Ontario Bar Association, 2004), the authors note, at 16:

Allegations of
cause for dismissal are subject to high scrutiny by the courts.  Adequate proof
of cause is generally required prior to dismissal and in some instances
following a thorough investigation.  Regardless of whether an employee is
forced to seek medical attention, employees have been awarded damages as a
result of improper accusations of dishonesty.

[182]

Thus, an unfounded allegation of cause can attract
Wallace

factor damages for the wrongfulness of the employer’s conduct, notwithstanding
an employee’s decision to seek medical attention for mental distress: see
Squires
v. Corner Book Pulp and Paper
(1999),
1999 CanLII 18967 (NL SC)
,
175 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 202
,

44 C.C.E.L. (2d) 246

(Nfld. S.C. (A.D.)).

[183]

Mr. Geluch claims additional damages to compensate him for what
he alleges was the unfair and harsh manner of his dismissal by Rosedale.  He
says that he was summarily fired, after twelve years of service and at the age
of fifty-four years, without warning and without explanation.  He says that he
was deprived of any opportunity to respond to the allegations made about him.
Furthermore, his chances of pursuing a career as a General Manager of a social
club were reduced significantly by Rosedale’s conduct.  Mr. Geluch submits that
the manner of his dismissal and the bad faith shown by Rosedale justify a
further period of notice of six months.

[184]

Mr. Geluch testified that he was told at 4:00 p.m. on Friday
October 31, 1997 that he was being dismissed.  He was not told the reasons for
the dismissal.  He was required to give over his keys and credit card.  He was
escorted out of the building.  I find that, at the time of his dismissal, some
staff members were still attending a party for a retiree across the hall from
the General Manager’s office.  The Clubhouse Manager and Executive Chef
witnessed Mr. Geluch’s departure.  Mr. Geluch described the incident as “the
most devastating day of my life… I felt my self-worth was totally destroyed… I
felt totally empty.  I had dedicated my life to Rosedale.  I had no respect
from them.  It was extremely difficult.  I felt like someone kicked me in the
stomach… I was absolutely stunned.  My thought process was not logical.”

[185]

Mr. Geluch testified that he went home to an empty house, as his
marriage had broken up and he was living alone at the time.  He called his
oldest friend in Vancouver for assistance.  Mr. Geluch was not given
out-placement counselling.  He was not provided with a letter of reference.  He
did not learn of the reasons for his dismissal until February 1998.

[186]

In his claim for damages arising from alleged bad faith, Mr.
Geluch also relied upon Rosedale’s conduct following his departure.  After Mr.
Geluch was dismissed, the President of Rosedale sent a letter to all the
members.  It stated that Michael Geluch had left the Club, and it advised
members that the functions of the General Manager would be performed on an
interim basis by a Committee consisting of Mr. Cowie, Mr. Hearne, and Mr.
Newbould.  Early in 1998, the President wrote a letter to approximately 1,300
members enclosing the Directors’ Report about the financial position of the
Club, and the 1997 financial statements.  Mr. Geluch alleges that the statement
“We already had concerns about the overall effectiveness of the Club’s Senior
Management” reflected negatively on him.

[187]

Mr. Geluch testified that the club industry is a small community
and that other clubs would have become aware of this message to the
membership.  According to Kathleen Mannion, the hospitality industry, and, in
particular, the club industry, is such that word gets around and would be
harmful to Mr. Geluch’s reputation.

[188]

Following Mr. Geluch’s departure from Rosedale, without going
into details, the Board attempted to convey to the membership that he had left
the organization and that Rosedale had had concerns about “former senior
management”.  I accept that a message to the membership with those words may
have had a negative impact on Mr. Geluch’s job search, particularly in light of
the industry in which he was employed.  Given the circumstances surrounding his
dismissal and the manner in which it was handled, I am satisfied that Mr.
Geluch is entitled to an additional notice period of two months for “Wallace”
damages.

b.
The
Claim for Aggravated Damages:

[189]

Aggravated damages are designed to compensate the employee for
intangible injuries suffered as a result of an actionable wrong.  In
Vorvis
,

supra
at paras.
21-22
, Justice McIntyre, speaking for the majority,
said:

From the foregoing authorities, I
would conclude that while aggravated damages may be awarded in actions for
breach of contract in appropriate cases, this is not a case where they should
be given.  The rule long established in the
Addis
and
Peso Silver
Mines
cases has generally been applied to deny such damages and the
employer/employee relationship … has always been one where either party could
terminate the contract of employment by due notice, and therefore the only
damage which could arise would result from a failure to give such a notice.

I would not wish
to be taken as saying that aggravated damages could never be awarded in a case
of wrongful dismissal, particularly where the acts complained of were also
independently actionable, a factor not present here.

[190]

Justice McIntyre concluded that aggravated damages could be
awarded where: (1) an employer’s conduct was independently actionable, (2) it
amounted to a wrong that was separate from the breach of contract for failure
to give reasonable notice of termination, and (3) it arose from the dismissal
itself, rather than the employer’s conduct before or after the dismissal. These
criteria were also considered in
Wallace
, where the majority recognized
that aggravated damages could be awarded for mental distress following a
wrongful dismissal.

[191]

However, in
Wallace
,
supra
at para.
73
, while the court
held that an award of damages beyond compensation for breach of an employment
contract “must be founded on a separately actionable course of conduct,” the
majority rejected the argument that a breach of the employer’s duty of good
faith to the employee at the time of the dismissal, by being untruthful or by
being unduly insensitive in the manner of dismissal, constituted an independent
actionable wrong.  Iacobucci J., for the majority, also rejected the creation
of a tort of “bad faith discharge”.  Instead, as is explained above, the
majority held that the notice period could be extended if, in dismissing the
employee, the employer engaged in conduct that was unfair or in bad faith.
Thus, while insensitivity may ground an extension of the notice period, it is
not, by itself, sufficient for an award of aggravated damages.

[192]

The elements of intentional infliction of mental suffering are:
“(1) flagrant or outrageous conduct, (2) calculated to produce harm, and (3)
resulting in a visible and provable illness”:
Zorn-Smith v. Bank of Montreal
,

supra
at para. 166;
Prinzo v. Baycrest Centre for Geriatric Care

(2002),
2002 CanLII 45005 (ON CA)
, 60 O.R. (3d) 474 at para.
48
(C.A.).  A reckless disregard as to
whether or not harm would ensure from the conduct, a desire to produce the
consequences that follow from the act, or if the consequences are known to be
substantially certain to follow, will all meet the intent requirement.

[193]

Applying the relevant law that is described above, I am not
satisfied that the plaintiff has established a separate actionable wrong to
support a claim for aggravated damages.

c.
The
Claim for Punitive Damages:

[194]

In
Vorvis
,
supra
at para.
16
, McIntyre J. stated:

Punitive
damages, as the name would indicate, are designed to punish. In this, they
constitute an exception to the general common law rule that damages are
designed to compensate the injured, not to punish the wrongdoer. Aggravated
damages will frequently cover conduct which could also be the subject of
punitive damages, but the role of aggravated damages remains compensatory.

[195]

As with aggravated damages, McIntyre J. held that punitive
damages may be awarded only where the defendant’s conduct constituted a
separate, actionable wrong, independent of the dismissal itself.  He added, at
para. 27:

Moreover, punitive damages may only be awarded in respect of conduct
which is of such nature as to be deserving of punishment because of its harsh,
vindictive, reprehensible and malicious nature. I do not suggest that I have
exhausted the adjectives which could describe the conduct capable of
characterizing a punitive award, but in any case where such an award is made
the conduct must be extreme in its nature and such that by any reasonable
standard it is deserving of full condemnation and punishment.

[196]

In
Hill v. Church of Scientology of Toronto
(1994),
1994 CanLII 10572 (ON CA)
, 18
O.R. (3d) 385 at 457, 114 D.L.R. (4
th
) 1 at 70 (C.A.), aff’d
1995 CanLII 59 (SCC)
, [1995]
2 S.C.R. 1130,
24 O.R. (3d) 865
, the
court held that punitive damages should only be awarded “if the compensatory
damages are considered by the jury to be insufficient to express its repugnance
at the conduct of the defendant and to punish and deter.”  In other words,
punitive damages are rarely awarded, and, when they are, they “must serve a
rational purpose”:
Whiten v. Pilot Insurance Co.
,
2002 SCC 18 (CanLII)
, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 595 at
paras.
101-2
,
209 D.L.R. (4th) 257
;

Marshall v. Watson Wyatt & Co.
,
supra
at para.
45
;
Antonacci
v. Great Atlantic & Pacific
Co. of Canada
,
supra
at para. 52.

[197]

In
Whiten v. Pilot
,
supra
, the Supreme Court of
Canada upheld a jury’s award of $1 million in punitive damages, approximately
three times the compensatory damages, against an insurer who had sought to deny
benefits to the insured family after their family home burned to the ground.
The court expanded on the “rationality test” from
Hill
,
supra
,
adding, at paras. 43 and 123, that it applies both to the question of whether
an award of punitive damages should be made at all, as well as to the question
of its quantum, thus keeping the award proportionate to such factors as the
harm caused, the degree of the misconduct, the relative vulnerability of the
plaintiff and any advantage or profit gained by the defendant.

[198]

In
Ben David v. Congregation B’nai Israel
(1999),
1999 CanLII 14854 (ON CTGD)
,
86 O.T.C. 45
,
44 C.C.E.L. (2d) 302

(Ont. Ct. Gen. Div.), the employer’s unfounded allegation of cause, although
withdrawn on the eve of trial, was nonetheless held to have been a malicious
attack justifying a punitive damages award of $20,000.  Other cases include:
Pilato
v. Hamilton Place Convention Centre Inc.
(1984),
1984 CanLII 1909 (ON HCJ)
, 45 O.R. (2d) 652, 7 D.L.R.
(4
th
) 342 (H.C.J.) (plaintiff awarded $25,000 in punitive damages
after being unfairly and severely dismissed);
Thom v. Goodhost Foods Ltd.
(1987),
17 C.C.E.L. 89 (H.C.J.)
(plaintiff awarded $20,000 in light of the
“scandalous”, unsupported allegations made by the employer, but abandoned at
the outset of trial);
Ribeiro v. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce

(1992),
1992 CanLII 7447 (ON CA)
, 13 O.R. (3d) 278,
44 C.C.E.L. 165

(C.A.), leave to appeal to the Supreme Court dismissed
[1993] S.C.C.A. No. 5

(appellate court increased the quantum of punitive damages to $50,000 to punish
and deter the type of “harsh, vindictive, reprehensible and malicious conduct”
of the respondents);
Williams v. Motorola Ltd
(1996),
1996 CanLII 8131 (ON CTGD)
,
18 C.C.E.L. (2d) 74

(Ont. Gen. Div.) (the plaintiff was awarded $20,000 in punitive damages after
she was wrongfully dismissed with no prior notice in order to avoid paying her
a bonus); and
Gilbert v. TS Realty Inc.
(1996),
1996 CanLII 8160 (ON CTGD)
,
13 O.T.C. 41
,
23 C.C.E.L. (2d) 100

(Ont. Gen. Div.) (the plaintiff was awarded $15,000 in punitive damages after
his wrongful dismissal caused him to be depressed, as was foreseeable).

[199]

With respect to punitive damages, Mr. Geluch claims that he is
entitled to punitive damages in the range of $50,000 to $75,000 for the harsh
and vindictive conduct exhibited by Rosedale.  In my view, the only possible
independent actionable wrong on the part of Rosedale would be a claim of
defamation arising from the covering letter sent by the President to the
membership along with the financial statements.  However, no such claim was
pleaded in this action.  Furthermore, the defendant may have had a good defence
to such an action.  Finally, the circumstances of the dismissal do not amount
to the type of conduct deserving of punishment because of its harsh,
vindictive, reprehensible and malicious nature.  For these reasons, the claim
for punitive damages does not succeed.

c.

The Claim for Accumulated Untaken Vacation Days
:

[200]

As part of his claim for damages, Mr. Geluch claims compensation
for accumulated unused vacation days.  Until 1995, Mr. Geluch was entitled to
four weeks of paid vacation.  From 1995 until his dismissal, he was entitled to
five weeks of paid vacation each year.  However, he did not use all his
allotted vacation time.

[201]

Mr. Geluch testified that he was aware that there was a policy in
the Club’s Handbook for Employees that employees could not accrue vacation days
from year to year without prior arrangements with their manager.  Ms. Nettleton
also confirmed that the policy prohibited carrying over vacation time unless
special permission was given.  However, when he testified, Mr. Geluch said he
did not believe that this policy applied to him, because he was the Senior
Executive of Rosedale and it was difficult for him to take his vacation, given
his extensive responsibilities.

[202]

Mr. Geluch testified that he had not taken a total of twenty-one
weeks of vacation for the period from 1988 to 1996 inclusive.  Mr. Geluch now
seeks compensation for these accrued vacation days, to be based upon his salary
in place at the relevant times.  Rosedale maintains that Mr. Geluch was bound
by the “use it or lose it” policy.  However, there was evidence led that
another employee had been paid for accrued vacation.  Furthermore, the
Employment
Standards Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. E.14 (since replaced by the
Employment
Standards Act
,

S.O. 2000, c. 41, s.38
) prohibits a “use it or lose
it” policy.  In light of the statutory provisions, Mr. Geluch is entitled to be
compensated for untaken accrued vacation pay for the twenty-one weeks, the
value of which I fix at $50,000.

d.

The Claim for Mitigation Expenses:

[203]

Mr. Geluch seeks compensation for costs he incurred in mitigating
his damages.  Following his dismissal from Rosedale, Mr. Geluch says that he
sent out numerous letters and made applications for positions within the club
and hospitality industry.  At trial, he submitted a list of  expenses which
include the cost of real estate commission and legal fees on the sale of his
Toronto home, the penalty for prepayment of his mortgage, the cost of an
airline ticket to Vancouver, the cost of transporting his car to British
Columbia, the cost of a car inspection, moving costs, telephone connection fees
in British Columbia, and miscellaneous expenses for photocopies and courier.
Counsel for Rosedale did not dispute the quantum but argued that since Mr.
Geluch received a capital gain of $27,500 on the sale of his Toronto house, any
mitigation expenses are offset.

[204]

In reviewing the expenses claimed, I agree that those expenses
related to the sale of his Toronto house should be offset against any capital
gains he made in that regard.  As those expenses are not consequential upon Mr.
Geluch’s dismissal and would have been incurred after the reasonable period of
notice in any event, they are not recoverable.  The remaining expenses such as
airfare to British Columbia, costs for transporting the car, the licence fee,
moving, and telephone connection are related to his dismissal from Rosedale,
are reasonable and should be recoverable.  I fix mitigation expenses at $8,000.

VIII.
COUNTERCLAIM:

[205]

Rosedale has counterclaimed for the clothing allowance claimed by
Mr. Geluch during the years 1993 to 1997, for the cost of Mr. Geluch’s personal
airfare and for $500 worth of furniture built for Mr. Geluch but not paid by
him.  In light of the evidence led at trial, the defendant has proven on a
balance of probabilities that the plaintiff owes monies for furniture built on
Club time and with the Club’s materials.  The defendant agrees that the value
is $500.  I grant judgment in the counterclaim for this amount which is owing
by the plaintiff.

IX.
SUMMARY
OF CONCLUSIONS:

[206]

For the reasons outlined above, I find that Michael Geluch was
dismissed from his employment as General Manager of Rosedale without just cause
at law.  In the circumstances, he was entitled to a reasonable period of
notice.  I find that the appropriate period of notice was fifteen months.  At
the time of his dismissal, Mr. Geluch was earning a salary of approximately
$129,000, and he is entitled to damages representing this annual total
compensation for fifteen months, plus the value of his benefits (which I fix at
15% of salary).  I fix the amount of $185,437.50 as the amount of salary and
benefits owing for the fifteen month period.  In light of the circumstances and
manner of his dismissal, he is entitled to a further two months’ notice and I
fix “Wallace” damages at $24,725.

[207]

For the reasons outlined above, the claim for twenty-one weeks’
of accumulated untaken vacation is granted and is fixed at $50,000.  The claim
for mitigation expenses reasonably incurred by Mr. Geluch is allowed at
$8,000.  Mr. Geluchi is entitled to salary and benefits during the notice period
less the value of his earnings at the Seymour Golf and Country Club for a two
month period.  As the parties did not lead that evidence, they are in the
position to calculate that deduction. The counterclaim by the defendant is
allowed at $500.

[208]

I also find that Mr. Geluch has not demonstrated on a balance of
probabilities that the conduct of Rosedale was such that he is entitled to
aggravated damages nor that the conduct was so harsh and vindictive that it
justifies the imposition of punitive damages.  The total amount owing to the
plaintiff is $267,662.50 less his earnings from the Seymour Golf and Country
Club.

[209]
